questions.stem: Two otherwise identical vascular beds are perfused by the same pressure gradient. The radius of vessels in bed X is 10% smaller than in bed Y. Which statement best predicts blood flow through bed X using Poiseuille principles?
options: Flow about 19% lower
Flow about 10% lower
Flow about 41% lower
Flow unchanged
Flow about 34% lower
questions.why: With the other variables fixed, **flow is proportional to radius to the fourth power**. The new flow is 0.9⁴ = 0.6561 of baseline: a 34.4% reduction.
distractors: This uses the change in cross-sectional area, 0.9 squared, rather than the flow relationship.
This treats flow as proportional to radius, ignoring the fourth power.
The new flow is about 66% of baseline, not 59%.
The pressure gradient is unchanged, but resistance has increased.
lo: Discuss the factors influencing blood flow, including the effect of the size of the blood vessel lumen, and its consequences for changes in blood flow distribution
sources: OpenStax: Blood flow, blood pressure and resistance — https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-2-blood-flow-blood-pressure-and-resistance
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Hypertension).

explanation: With pressure held constant, the difference in flow comes from resistance; an increased driving pressure cannot compensate.

keyClues.quote: radius of vessels in bed X is 10% smaller
explanation: Flow is proportional to radius to the fourth power. 0.9⁴ = 0.6561, so flow falls by approximately 34%, not 10% or 19%.

keyConcept.summary: With the other variables fixed, flow is proportional to radius to the fourth power
paragraphs: Poiseuille’s relationship assumes laminar flow through a cylindrical tube. It explains why modest changes in arteriolar radius can redistribute flow substantially. Calculate the remaining fraction first, then subtract it from one to find the reduction.

commonTraps: Do not report 66% as the reduction: it is the flow remaining.
recogniseNextTime: Convert the percentage reduction into a radius ratio before applying the fourth power.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Would resistance rise or fall?
followUpQuestions.answer: It rises: with pressure unchanged, lower flow means greater resistance.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: With the other variables fixed, flow is proportional to radius to the fourth power

questions.stem: A patient reports intermittent wheeze. A well-performed twice-daily peak-flow diary shows readings that fall during symptoms and recover between episodes. What does this pattern principally demonstrate?
options: Persistent loss of elastic recoil
Reduced alveolar gas-transfer capacity
A fixed reduction in total lung capacity
Increased residual volume on every measurement
Variable expiratory airflow limitation
questions.why: The diary supports **variable expiratory airflow limitation**, a characteristic feature of asthma when consistent with the clinical history.
distractors: This is associated with emphysema and does not best explain symptom-linked reversibility.
Gas transfer requires a different measurement; peak flow measures expiratory flow.
Peak flow does not measure total lung capacity, and the changing readings argue against a purely fixed deficit.
Peak flow does not directly measure residual volume.
lo: Describe how asthma can be diagnosed, including symptoms, signs and investigations
sources: Recommendations | Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management (BTS, NICE, SIGN) | Guidance | NICE — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng245/chapter/recommendations
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Introduction).

explanation: An episodic symptom pattern suggests fluctuating airway narrowing, although the symptom alone does not establish asthma.

keyClues.quote: fall during symptoms and recover between episodes
explanation: The measured variable is peak expiratory flow. Its reversibility supports variable airflow limitation; this diary does not measure lung volumes or gas transfer.

keyConcept.summary: The diary supports variable expiratory airflow limitation, a characteristic feature of asthma when consistent with the clinical history.
paragraphs: Peak expiratory flow is effort-dependent. Consistent technique and repeated readings make a diary more informative than a single low result. Objective variability supports the diagnosis but should be interpreted with history and other testing.

commonTraps: Peak flow is not a direct measurement of lung volume or diffusion.
recogniseNextTime: Recovery separates variability from a consistently reduced flow measurement.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why record readings when asymptomatic too?
followUpQuestions.answer: They provide a comparison that can reveal variability over time.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The diary supports variable expiratory airflow limitation, a characteristic feature of asthma when consistent with the clinical history.

questions.stem: A loop diuretic inhibits NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Which normal transport process is directly reduced?
options: Glucose-coupled sodium uptake in the proximal tubule
Sodium entry through ENaC in the collecting duct
NaCl reabsorption in a water-impermeable segment
ADH-regulated water entry through aquaporin-2
NaCl reabsorption through NCC in the distal convoluted tubule
questions.why: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs salt without accompanying water. **NKCC2 inhibition** reduces this transport and weakens the medullary concentrating gradient.
distractors: This involves SGLT transporters rather than NKCC2.
ENaC is a different channel in a different nephron segment.
This occurs in collecting-duct principal cells, not through NKCC2.
NCC is the thiazide target.
lo: Explain the mechanisms of tubular reabsorption and secretion in relation to hormonal control and diuretic action
sources: OpenStax: Tubular reabsorption — https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/25-6-tubular-reabsorption
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Acute Kidney Injury.

explanation: Locate the segment before matching the transporter to a drug class.

keyConcept.summary: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs salt without accompanying water
paragraphs: Water permeability differs along the nephron. Salt removal in the ascending limb both dilutes tubular fluid and supports the medullary gradient used elsewhere to reclaim water. This links a local transporter effect to whole-kidney concentrating ability.

commonTraps: Do not swap the loop NKCC2 transporter with distal NCC.
recogniseNextTime: Locate the segment before matching the transporter to a drug class.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which class inhibits NCC?
followUpQuestions.answer: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs salt without accompanying water

questions.stem: A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick from blood known to contain hepatitis virus. Which pair of hepatitis viruses is most characteristically associated with blood-borne transmission rather than the faeco-oral route?
options: Hepatitis A and B
Hepatitis D and E
Hepatitis B and C
Hepatitis A and E
Hepatitis C and E
questions.why: **Hepatitis B and C** are major blood-borne hepatitis viruses. Hepatitis A and E are mainly transmitted by enteric routes.
distractors: This combines one predominantly enteric virus with one blood-borne virus.
D depends on HBV and can be blood-borne, but E makes this pair incorrect.
Both are predominantly enterically transmitted.
Hepatitis E is mainly enterically transmitted, so the pair is not the best fit.
lo: Describe the risk factors, epidemiology and control measures for hepatitis A, B, C, D and E
sources: Hepatitis — https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/hepatitis
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Hepatobiliary).

explanation: Blood exposure is the relevant route being tested.

keyConcept.summary: Hepatitis B and C are major blood-borne hepatitis viruses
paragraphs: Transmission route, chronicity and prevention are separate properties. Hepatitis D requires hepatitis B surface antigen, while hepatitis C does not. This question identifies a route pairing rather than prescribing post-exposure management.

commonTraps: Do not exclude hepatitis D from blood-borne transmission; it is the E component that makes that pair wrong.
recogniseNextTime: Blood exposure is the relevant route being tested.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which hepatitis virus depends on hepatitis B?
followUpQuestions.answer: Hepatitis D.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Hepatitis B and C are major blood-borne hepatitis viruses

questions.stem: A patient has fatigue, cold intolerance, a raised TSH and low free T4. Which location of dysfunction best explains the hormone pattern?
options: Autonomous thyroid hormone secretion
Pituitary failure reducing TSH secretion
Primary thyroid gland failure
A TSH-secreting pituitary tumour
Hypothalamic failure reducing TRH secretion
questions.why: Low T4 with **appropriately raised TSH** indicates primary hypothyroidism: the pituitary is trying to stimulate an underperforming thyroid.
distractors: This generally raises thyroid hormone and suppresses TSH.
This would give a low or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4.
This typically produces raised thyroid hormone with non-suppressed TSH.
This also fails to produce the appropriate high TSH response.
lo: Describe the synthesis, metabolism and actions of hormones of the hypothalamic pituitary axis using thyroid hormones as an example
sources: Hypothyroidism - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519536/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

explanation: Low circulating thyroid hormone establishes the hypothyroid biochemical direction; autonomous secretion or a functioning TSH-secreting tumour would usually raise T4.
The pituitary is responding to reduced negative feedback. A high TSH with low T4 localises the main defect to the thyroid, rather than deficient hypothalamic or pituitary drive.

keyConcept.summary: Low T4 with appropriately raised TSH indicates primary hypothyroidism: the pituitary is trying to stimulate an underperforming thyroid.
paragraphs: Thyroid hormone normally suppresses hypothalamic and pituitary stimulation. Loss of thyroid output removes that feedback. A low T4 without a suitable TSH rise instead raises concern about central dysfunction.

commonTraps: A normal-range TSH can be inappropriate when T4 is low.
recogniseNextTime: Interpret both values together to locate the defect in the feedback axis.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What normally happens to TSH when free T4 rises?
followUpQuestions.answer: Negative feedback suppresses TSH.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Low T4 with appropriately raised TSH indicates primary hypothyroidism: the pituitary is trying to stimulate an underperforming thyroid.

questions.stem: Metformin lowers glucose without directly stimulating pancreatic insulin secretion. Which effect is most closely associated with its glucose-lowering action?
options: Closure of beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels
Inhibition of proximal tubular SGLT2
Reduced hepatic glucose production
Direct replacement of endogenous insulin
Inhibition of intestinal alpha-glucosidase
questions.why: Metformin reduces **hepatic glucose production** and improves aspects of insulin sensitivity without acting as a direct insulin secretagogue.
distractors: This describes sulfonylurea action.
This increases urinary glucose loss and is a different drug class.
Injected insulin supplies exogenous hormone; metformin changes glucose handling without replacing insulin.
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors delay intestinal carbohydrate digestion; this is not the main action of metformin.
lo: Understand the mechanism of action of commonly used antidiabetic medications.
sources: Revisiting the mechanisms of metformin action in the liver - PubMed — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23582849/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Metabolic Disorders (Diabetes).

keyClues.quote: without directly stimulating pancreatic insulin secretion
explanation: Exclude mechanisms that principally release stored insulin.

keyConcept.summary: Metformin reduces hepatic glucose production and improves aspects of insulin sensitivity without acting as a direct insulin secretagogue.
paragraphs: Glucose-lowering medicines act at different organs and pathways. Metformin’s cellular actions are complex, so a single simplified molecular target should not be presented as the complete mechanism. The organ-level effect is the appropriate focus here.

commonTraps: Do not describe every oral diabetes medicine as stimulating insulin release.
recogniseNextTime: Exclude mechanisms that principally release stored insulin.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which class directly closes beta-cell KATP channels?
followUpQuestions.answer: Sulfonylureas.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Metformin reduces hepatic glucose production and improves aspects of insulin sensitivity without acting as a direct insulin secretagogue.

questions.stem: During a primary systemic antibody response, the earliest substantial secreted antibody is detected before class switching. Which immunoglobulin class is most likely?
options: IgA
IgD
IgM
IgG
IgE
questions.why: **IgM** is typically the first major secreted class in a primary systemic response.
distractors: IgA is especially important at mucosal surfaces.
IgD is mainly a receptor on naive B cells rather than the main early secreted antibody.
IgG becomes prominent after class switching and in many secondary systemic responses.
IgE is associated with allergic responses and defence against helminths.
lo: Describe how pathogen recognition is achieved by antibodies and the distinctive roles that different classes of antibody have during an immune response
sources: Glossary - Immunobiology - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK10759/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Infections).

explanation: The timing and absence of class switching distinguish the early secreted response.

keyConcept.summary: IgM is typically the first major secreted class in a primary systemic response.
paragraphs: Membrane-bound IgM and IgD help naive B cells recognise antigen. Secreted IgM is usually pentameric, providing multiple binding sites. Antibody class switching changes the constant region and effector function while preserving antigen specificity.

commonTraps: Do not confuse a surface B-cell receptor with the dominant secreted serum class.
recogniseNextTime: The timing and absence of class switching distinguish the early secreted response.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Does class switching usually change antigen specificity?
followUpQuestions.answer: No; it principally changes the constant region and associated effector functions.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: IgM is typically the first major secreted class in a primary systemic response.

questions.stem: Unfractionated heparin rapidly reduces the activity of thrombin and factor Xa. Which circulating protein must it bind to produce its main anticoagulant effect?
options: Protein S
von Willebrand factor
Plasminogen
Antithrombin
Protein C
questions.why: Heparin binds **antithrombin**, accelerating inhibition of activated coagulation factors, particularly thrombin and factor Xa.
distractors: Protein S supports activated protein C rather than mediating heparin action.
This supports platelet adhesion and carries factor VIII.
Activation of plasminogen promotes fibrin breakdown, a fibrinolytic mechanism.
Activated protein C degrades factors Va and VIIIa; it is not the principal heparin-binding cofactor.
questions.module: Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease)
lo: Outline the clotting cascade in order to explain the mechanism of action of anti-coagulant and anti-platelet drugs
sources: StatPearls: Heparin — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538247/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease).

explanation: Rapid inhibition of existing activated factors differs from reducing synthesis of new clotting factors.

keyConcept.summary: Heparin binds antithrombin, accelerating inhibition of activated coagulation factors, particularly thrombin and factor Xa.
paragraphs: Anticoagulants limit formation and extension of thrombi. They do not directly dissolve an established fibrin clot; that requires fibrinolysis. Unfractionated heparin can inhibit both thrombin and Xa through antithrombin.

commonTraps: Do not confuse anticoagulation with plasmin-mediated clot breakdown.
recogniseNextTime: Rapid inhibition of existing activated factors differs from reducing synthesis of new clotting factors.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How does warfarin differ in timing?
followUpQuestions.answer: Its effect develops as existing vitamin K-dependent clotting factors turn over.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.curriculumSource: LOs/Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease) - LOs.txt
questions.assessmentObjective: Heparin binds antithrombin, accelerating inhibition of activated coagulation factors, particularly thrombin and factor Xa.

questions.stem: A healthy adult briefly reduces alveolar ventilation. Which change most directly stimulates the central chemoreceptors to increase ventilation?
options: Increased plasma hydrogen ions crossing the blood–brain barrier rapidly
Decreased arterial CO2 sensed in the carotid bodies
Increased bicarbonate concentration in cerebrospinal fluid
Decreased arterial oxygen sensed directly by medullary neurons
Increased hydrogen ion concentration in brain extracellular fluid after CO2 entry
questions.why: Retained CO2 enters the brain and generates hydrogen ions. **Central chemoreceptors respond to the local fall in pH**, increasing ventilatory drive.
distractors: CO2 crosses readily; hydrogen ions do not do so to the same extent.
Hypoventilation raises CO2; carotid bodies are peripheral receptors.
Buffering hydrogen ions would oppose, rather than explain, the acute stimulus.
Arterial hypoxaemia is principally detected by peripheral chemoreceptors.
lo: Describe the process of ventilation, the mechanisms used to control respiration, and how these are affected by lung disease
sources: Central Chemoreceptors: Locations and Functions - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4802370/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Introduction).

explanation: Reduced ventilation retains CO2, rather than lowering arterial CO2.

CO2 crosses into the brain and generates hydrogen ions locally. Direct sensing of low arterial oxygen chiefly involves peripheral chemoreceptors; plasma hydrogen ions do not rapidly cross the blood–brain barrier.

keyConcept.summary: Retained CO2 enters the brain and generates hydrogen ions
paragraphs: Distinguish the substance that crosses into the brain from the local chemical stimulus. Peripheral carotid and aortic bodies contribute additional information, especially about arterial oxygen, CO2 and pH.

commonTraps: Do not describe the central chemoreceptors as the main direct oxygen sensors.
recogniseNextTime: Reduced CO2 elimination is the initiating change.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What happens to arterial CO2 during hyperventilation?
followUpQuestions.answer: It falls as alveolar CO2 elimination increases.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Retained CO2 enters the brain and generates hydrogen ions

questions.stem: A child develops oedema and cola-coloured urine after a streptococcal infection. Renal biopsy shows granular immunoglobulin and complement deposits in glomeruli. Which mechanism best explains the renal injury?
options: Antibody binding directly along the glomerular basement membrane
IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation
Immune-complex-mediated inflammation
Cytotoxic T-cell injury without antibody deposition
Failure of neutrophil oxidative killing
questions.why: **Immune complexes activate complement and inflammation**, producing a type III hypersensitivity pattern of glomerular injury.
distractors: Anti-GBM disease characteristically gives a linear staining pattern.
This produces immediate allergic responses rather than granular glomerular deposits.
This does not explain the immunoglobulin and complement pattern.
This predisposes to infection but is not the deposited-complex mechanism.
lo: Explain how a post-streptococcal renal failure relates to the Gel and Coombs classification of hypersensitivity reactions (Types I-IV)
sources: Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis - Streptococcus pyogenes - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK333429/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Acute Kidney Injury.

explanation: This suggests glomerular bleeding in this context; paired with oedema it supports a nephritic presentation.
The preceding infection provides a trigger for a post-infectious immune response rather than proving direct bacterial invasion of the glomeruli.
Granular deposits support immune-complex deposition. Direct anti-GBM antibody binding typically gives a linear pattern; a purely T-cell process would not explain these antibody deposits.

keyConcept.summary: Immune complexes activate complement and inflammation, producing a type III hypersensitivity pattern of glomerular injury.
paragraphs: Post-infectious glomerulonephritis can cause haematuria, fluid retention and reduced filtration. The immune mechanism is distinct from direct bacterial invasion of glomeruli. Complement consumption may accompany the inflammatory process.

commonTraps: Do not classify every antibody-associated injury as type II.
recogniseNextTime: Granular deposits support complexes rather than the linear pattern of anti-GBM disease.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What staining pattern suggests anti-GBM disease instead?
followUpQuestions.answer: Linear immunoglobulin staining along the basement membrane.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Immune complexes activate complement and inflammation, producing a type III hypersensitivity pattern of glomerular injury.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has ascites, portal hypertension and low serum albumin. Which paired pressure changes favour fluid leaving splanchnic capillaries?
options: Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure and lower plasma oncotic pressure
Lower capillary hydrostatic pressure and higher plasma oncotic pressure
Unchanged hydrostatic pressure and higher plasma oncotic pressure
Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure and higher plasma oncotic pressure
Lower capillary hydrostatic pressure and lower plasma oncotic pressure
questions.why: **Raised hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out**, while reduced albumin weakens the oncotic force retaining it in plasma.
distractors: Both changes favour retention in the circulation.
This does not account for either stated abnormality.
The oncotic change would oppose fluid leaving the circulation.
The hydrostatic change would oppose outward filtration.
lo: Describe the pathophysiology of cirrhosis and portal hypertension, relating these to the symptoms and the signs of the disease
sources: Ascites - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470482/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Hepatobiliary).

explanation: Raised venous pressure increases upstream splanchnic capillary hydrostatic pressure, favouring outward filtration.
Albumin contributes to plasma oncotic pressure. A lower concentration reduces the force retaining water in the circulation; it does not raise oncotic pressure.

keyConcept.summary: Raised hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, while reduced albumin weakens the oncotic force retaining it in plasma.
paragraphs: Ascites in cirrhosis is more complex than two pressures alone: altered splanchnic circulation and renal sodium retention also contribute. The question isolates the direction of the specified forces rather than claiming a complete explanation of the syndrome.

commonTraps: Keep hydrostatic pressure and oncotic pressure separate.
recogniseNextTime: The stem supplies one change on each side of the fluid-balance relationship.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which plasma protein contributes most to oncotic pressure?
followUpQuestions.answer: Albumin.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Raised hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, while reduced albumin weakens the oncotic force retaining it in plasma.

questions.stem: A patient with untreated diabetes has marked hyperglycaemia, glycosuria and polyuria. Which process most directly causes the large urinary water loss?
options: Osmotic retention of water by unreabsorbed tubular glucose
Increased ADH action making the collecting duct water-impermeable
Reduced plasma osmolality suppressing thirst
Complete suppression of glomerular filtration
Increased sodium retention eliminating the medullary gradient
questions.why: Filtered glucose that exceeds reabsorptive capacity remains in tubular fluid and causes **osmotic diuresis**. Water and electrolyte losses can be substantial.
distractors: ADH increases water permeability rather than decreasing it.
Hyperglycaemia raises, rather than lowers, extracellular osmolality.
Stopping filtration would reduce urine formation.
This does not describe the glucose-linked mechanism in the stem.
lo: Explain the physiological changes in body fluid balance occurring in diabetic keto-acidosis
sources: Hyperglycemic Crises - Endotext - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279052/?report=reader
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Metabolic Disorders (Diabetes).

explanation: Filtered glucose exceeds reabsorptive capacity and remains in the tubular lumen, where it retains water osmotically.
Large urine output requires ongoing filtration and water loss. Complete suppression of GFR would reduce output, while ADH normally increases collecting-duct water permeability.

keyConcept.summary: Filtered glucose that exceeds reabsorptive capacity remains in tubular fluid and causes osmotic diuresis
paragraphs: A high extracellular glucose concentration can coexist with severe dehydration. Thirst is compensatory, but intake may not keep pace with urinary losses. This fluid mechanism is distinct from the ketone production responsible for DKA acidosis.

commonTraps: High blood glucose does not mean the body is retaining enough water.
recogniseNextTime: Glucose in the urine provides the osmotic link between high blood glucose and urinary water loss.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why can total body potassium be depleted in DKA?
followUpQuestions.answer: Urinary losses can deplete stores even when the measured serum concentration is normal or high.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Filtered glucose that exceeds reabsorptive capacity remains in tubular fluid and causes osmotic diuresis

questions.stem: After a meal, insulin-resistant skeletal muscle takes up less glucose despite a high circulating insulin concentration. Which cellular defect most directly contributes?
options: Increased GLUT4 insertion into the surface membrane
Reduced insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation
Reduced glucose filtration at the glomerulus
Increased sodium–glucose cotransport at the muscle membrane
Reduced GLUT2 expression on the muscle surface
questions.why: Insulin normally promotes **GLUT4 movement to the cell surface**. Impaired signalling reduces this response and postprandial glucose disposal.
distractors: That would increase insulin-stimulated uptake rather than reduce it.
That is a renal process and does not explain the muscle-cell defect.
Skeletal-muscle uptake is not primarily mediated by intestinal-type SGLT transport.
GLUT4 is the main insulin-responsive transporter in skeletal muscle.
lo: Explain the mechanism for maintaining glucose homeostasis and its relationship with lipid metabolism and insulin resistance
sources: Physiology, Glucose Transporter Type 4 - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537322/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Metabolic Disorders (Obesity).

explanation: Insulin-responsive glucose uptake in muscle principally uses GLUT4, rather than renal sodium–glucose cotransport or GLUT2.

keyClues.quote: less glucose despite a high circulating insulin concentration
explanation: There is reduced response to available insulin, supporting impaired GLUT4 translocation rather than increased membrane insertion.

keyConcept.summary: Insulin normally promotes GLUT4 movement to the cell surface
paragraphs: Insulin resistance is reduced responsiveness to insulin, not necessarily absent insulin. Muscle is a major site of meal-related glucose disposal, so impaired uptake contributes to hyperglycaemia even while pancreatic secretion compensates.

commonTraps: Do not apply the same transporter mechanism to every cell type.
recogniseNextTime: The tissue matters: glucose transporters and insulin dependence differ between organs.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Name another insulin-responsive GLUT4 tissue.
followUpQuestions.answer: Adipose tissue.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Insulin normally promotes GLUT4 movement to the cell surface

questions.stem: A patient has anaemia, jaundice, increased unconjugated bilirubin and a high reticulocyte count. Which process best integrates these results?
options: Peripheral haemolysis with marrow compensation
Acute uncomplicated blood loss without red-cell destruction
Isolated impaired hepatic bilirubin conjugation
Iron-deficient erythropoiesis
Marrow failure
questions.why: **Accelerated red-cell destruction** produces bilirubin, while an intact marrow compensates by releasing more reticulocytes.
distractors: Reticulocytosis can follow bleeding, but the bilirubin pattern points more strongly to haemolysis.
This can raise unconjugated bilirubin but does not explain anaemia with a marrow response.
This is an underproduction process and does not best explain reticulocytosis with increased bilirubin.
Reticulocyte production would usually be low.
lo: Identify the clinical features of iron deficiency anaemia, pernicious anaemia and haemolytic anaemia relating to their underlying causes
sources: Hemolytic anemia - PubMed — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15202694/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Anaemia.

explanation: Increased haem breakdown supplies unconjugated bilirubin. This supports red-cell destruction rather than uncomplicated blood loss alone.
The marrow is responding by releasing young red cells. Marrow failure or untreated iron-limited production would not normally produce this compensatory response.
Combining anaemia with biochemical haem breakdown favours haemolysis; an isolated hepatic conjugation defect does not itself account for the anaemia.

keyConcept.summary: Accelerated red-cell destruction produces bilirubin, while an intact marrow compensates by releasing more reticulocytes.
paragraphs: Interpret the reticulocyte response in relation to the severity of anaemia; an apparently normal percentage may be inadequate. Haemolysis can be intravascular or extravascular, and further tests help identify its cause.

commonTraps: Jaundice alone does not establish haemolysis; combine it with the blood findings.
recogniseNextTime: Reticulocytosis distinguishes a compensating marrow from many underproduction states.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What typically happens to haptoglobin in intravascular haemolysis?
followUpQuestions.answer: It falls as it binds released haemoglobin.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Accelerated red-cell destruction produces bilirubin, while an intact marrow compensates by releasing more reticulocytes.

questions.stem: A patient develops a persistent dry cough after starting an ACE inhibitor. Which change most directly explains this adverse effect?
options: Direct stimulation of airway beta-2 receptors
Reduced breakdown of bradykinin
Increased conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
Direct blockade of muscarinic receptors
Increased aldosterone synthesis
questions.why: ACE also breaks down bradykinin. Inhibition can increase **bradykinin-related airway effects**, contributing to a dry cough.
distractors: This promotes bronchodilation and is not the cough mechanism.
ACE inhibition reduces that conversion.
This is not the ACE inhibitor target.
ACE inhibition generally reduces angiotensin-II-driven aldosterone release.
lo: Identify the mode of action and side effects of drugs used to treat heart failure including ACE inhibitors, digoxin, betablockers and diuretics
sources: StatPearls: ACE inhibitors — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430896/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

explanation: The medication timing and non-productive cough support a mechanism-based adverse effect.

paragraphs: ACE inhibition affects more than angiotensin production. This helps distinguish its adverse-effect profile from angiotensin-receptor blockade, which does not inhibit bradykinin breakdown in the same way. Other causes of cough still require consideration.

commonTraps: A cough after starting a medicine is a clue, not proof of causation.
recogniseNextTime: The medication timing and non-productive cough support a mechanism-based adverse effect.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why is cough less characteristic of an ARB?
followUpQuestions.answer: ARBs block the angiotensin II receptor without directly inhibiting ACE-mediated bradykinin breakdown.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.stem: A previously sensitised patient develops wheeze within minutes of inhaling a particular allergen. Which event initiates the immediate allergic response?
options: Activation of allergen-specific cytotoxic T cells
Deposition of IgG immune complexes in airway vessels
Binding of IgG to an intrinsic airway basement-membrane antigen
Cross-linking of mast-cell-bound IgE
Expansion of naive B-cell clones into antibody-secreting cells
questions.why: Allergen cross-links **IgE already bound to mast cells**, triggering mediator release and bronchoconstriction.
distractors: T-cell-mediated injury typically develops more slowly.
This describes an immune-complex mechanism, not the immediate sensitised response.
This is an antibody-mediated tissue-targeting mechanism rather than allergen-triggered mast-cell activation.
That takes longer than the minutes described.
lo: Explain and compare the immunological and pathological changes occurring in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma and how these result in the symptoms and signs of the disease
sources: IgE and mast cells: The endogenous adjuvant. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33190734/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Introduction).

explanation: Sensitisation allows allergen-specific IgE to occupy mast-cell Fc receptors before re-exposure.
The immediate response is release of preformed mediators after IgE cross-linking. New B-cell expansion and a delayed T-cell reaction take longer.

keyConcept.summary: Allergen cross-links IgE already bound to mast cells, triggering mediator release and bronchoconstriction.
paragraphs: The sensitisation phase establishes allergen-specific IgE. Re-exposure activates mast cells; a later inflammatory phase may involve eosinophils and other cells. The immediate and late phases are related but are not the same initiating event.

commonTraps: Do not choose a slow cellular response just because asthma also has chronic inflammation.
recogniseNextTime: The rapid timing implies pre-existing sensitisation and immediate mediator release.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which hypersensitivity category is this?
followUpQuestions.answer: Type I hypersensitivity.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Allergen cross-links IgE already bound to mast cells, triggering mediator release and bronchoconstriction.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced CKD has normocytic anaemia, a low reticulocyte count and adequate iron stores. Which impaired process most directly explains the reduced red-cell production?
options: Platelet-derived thrombopoietin production
Hepatic bilirubin conjugation
Renal erythropoietin production
Splenic clearance of senescent erythrocytes
Gastric intrinsic-factor production
questions.why: Damaged kidneys may produce insufficient **erythropoietin**, reducing the marrow stimulus for red-cell production.
distractors: Thrombopoietin chiefly regulates platelet production and is mainly produced by the liver.
This affects bilirubin handling rather than directly stimulating erythropoiesis.
Reduced clearance does not explain an underproduction pattern.
Loss of intrinsic factor leads to B12 deficiency and typically megaloblastic change.
lo: Describe the symptoms and signs of chronic kidney disease, explaining their causal mechanism in each case
sources: StatPearls: Anaemia of chronic kidney disease — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539871/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Chronic Kidney Injury.

explanation: Diseased kidneys may provide insufficient erythropoietin stimulation to the marrow, directly reducing erythropoiesis. Thrombopoietin regulates platelet production, while bilirubin conjugation processes haem breakdown products rather than stimulating red-cell production.

This is a poor production response to anaemia. Impaired splenic clearance would reduce removal of circulating red cells, not directly suppress marrow production. Conversely, increased peripheral destruction normally provokes reticulocytosis if the marrow can respond.
A normal mean cell volume fits the usual pattern of erythropoietin-deficient anaemia. Intrinsic-factor deficiency instead points towards B12 deficiency and often macrocytosis.
Iron depletion is not the explanation supplied here. CKD can still impair iron availability, but among these options deficient erythropoietin is the direct production defect.

keyConcept.summary: Damaged kidneys may produce insufficient erythropoietin, reducing the marrow stimulus for red-cell production.
paragraphs: CKD anaemia can be multifactorial, including inflammation and iron restriction. This stem removes obvious iron deficiency to isolate the endocrine contribution of the kidney. A normal MCV describes cell size, not a single diagnosis.

commonTraps: Do not assume all anaemia in CKD is solely due to iron loss.
recogniseNextTime: These findings support underproduction rather than a simple lack of iron or brisk compensation for haemolysis.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Would an intact marrow usually raise reticulocytes during haemolysis?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes, if it has adequate substrates and sufficient time to respond.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Damaged kidneys may produce insufficient erythropoietin, reducing the marrow stimulus for red-cell production.

questions.stem: A patient has chronic greasy stools and weight loss, and pancreatic exocrine insufficiency is suspected. Which stool investigation most directly assesses pancreatic digestive-enzyme output?
options: Faecal immunochemical test
Faecal alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance
Faecal calprotectin
Faecal elastase
Stool culture
questions.why: **Faecal elastase** provides an indirect measure of pancreatic exocrine secretion and is useful in suspected pancreatic insufficiency.
distractors: This detects human haemoglobin in stool, not pancreatic enzyme output.
This assesses intestinal protein loss rather than pancreatic secretion.
This is mainly a marker of intestinal inflammation.
This investigates enteric infection rather than exocrine function.
lo: Describe the common presenting symptoms of malabsorption, and explain the principles of common investigations including faecal elastase, jejunal biopsy and tissue transglutaminase antibodies
sources: NIDDK: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency — https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/exocrine-pancreatic-insufficiency
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Malabsorption).

keyClues.quote: chronic greasy stools and weight loss
explanation: These suggest maldigestion or malabsorption, but do not by themselves distinguish pancreatic from intestinal disease.
The question asks specifically about exocrine pancreatic function. Faecal elastase reflects a pancreatic enzyme; calprotectin assesses intestinal inflammation and FIT detects blood.

keyConcept.summary: Faecal elastase provides an indirect measure of pancreatic exocrine secretion and is useful in suspected pancreatic insufficiency.
paragraphs: Malabsorption has several causes, including mucosal disease, inadequate bile delivery and pancreatic enzyme deficiency. A low elastase result requires context; a very watery stool can dilute the measured concentration.

commonTraps: Faecal calprotectin and elastase investigate different processes.
recogniseNextTime: Match the test to the specific function, rather than simply to diarrhoea.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why can exocrine failure cause steatorrhoea?
followUpQuestions.answer: Insufficient digestive enzymes, especially lipase, impair fat digestion.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Faecal elastase provides an indirect measure of pancreatic exocrine secretion and is useful in suspected pancreatic insufficiency.

questions.stem: An early embryo contains an inner cell mass and a fluid-filled cavity surrounded by trophoblast. Which developmental stage is described?
options: Blastocyst
Morula
Gastrula
Neurula
Zygote
questions.why: A **blastocyst** has an inner cell mass, a cavity and an outer trophoblast layer and is the stage that begins implantation.
distractors: The morula is a solid cluster of blastomeres before a prominent cavity forms.
Gastrulation establishes the three embryonic germ layers later.
Neurulation concerns formation of the neural plate and tube later in development.
The zygote is the single-cell stage immediately after fertilisation.
lo: Describe in broad outline the stages of development of the embryo from conception to birth
sources: Early Mammalian Development - Developmental Biology - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK10052/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Start in Life.

explanation: This group will give rise to the embryo proper, helping identify the organised blastocyst rather than a single zygote.

keyClues.quote: a fluid-filled cavity surrounded by trophoblast
explanation: The blastocoel and surrounding trophoblast distinguish a blastocyst from a solid morula. Gastrulation and neurulation describe later developmental organisation.

keyConcept.summary: A blastocyst has an inner cell mass, a cavity and an outer trophoblast layer and is the stage that begins implantation.
paragraphs: Cleavage increases cell number before the morula develops into a blastocyst. The inner cell mass contributes to the embryo, while trophoblast contributes to placental structures. Implantation and gastrulation describe different events.

commonTraps: Do not label any early multicellular embryo a morula.
recogniseNextTime: Use structure rather than just memorising a time point.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What distinguishes a morula structurally?
followUpQuestions.answer: It is a solid ball of cells rather than a cavitated blastocyst.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: A blastocyst has an inner cell mass, a cavity and an outer trophoblast layer and is the stage that begins implantation.

questions.stem: During CBT for weight management, a patient says, “If I do not snack after a stressful shift, I will stay tense all evening.” A diary has established the pattern. Which agreed task would most directly test this prediction?
options: Try a ten-minute walk after a shift and compare predicted with actual tension before deciding whether to snack
Record snack portions and estimated calories after each shift for the next week
Keep snacks in a less accessible cupboard and prepare portions at the start of the week
List evidence for and against the thought that a difficult shift deserves a food reward
Choose a non-food reward for meeting an agreed weekly snack-frequency target
questions.why: A behavioural experiment tests a specific prediction against experience. Trying another response and comparing expected with actual tension tests whether snacking is necessary for the tension to settle.
distractors: Self-monitoring provides useful data, but this diary task does not test the prediction about remaining tense.
Stimulus control changes access and cues; it does not directly compare the predicted emotional outcome with what happens.
Cognitive restructuring examines a related appraisal. This task debates deserving a reward rather than testing the stated prediction in practice.
Reinforcement can support behaviour change, but achieving a frequency target does not directly test the prediction about tension.
lo: Discuss the psycho-social factors associated with weight gain and weight loss and explain the principles underpinning cognitive-behavioural weight loss programmes
sources: NICE NG246: Behavioural weight-management interventions — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246/chapter/Behavioural-overweight-and-obesity-management-interventions
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Metabolic Disorders (Obesity).

keyClues.quote: I will stay tense all evening
explanation: This is a testable prediction about what will happen if the usual behaviour changes.

keyClues.quote: A diary has established the pattern
explanation: The next task can move from monitoring to testing the maintaining belief.

keyConcept.summary: A behavioural experiment tests a specific prediction against experience. Trying another response and comparing expected with actual tension tests whether snacking is necessary for the tension to settle.
paragraphs: Match the CBT technique to its purpose: monitoring identifies patterns; an experiment tests a prediction.

The patient and clinician agree a feasible alternative, record the prediction, try it and review the result. The outcome may support or weaken the belief; success is learning, not simply meeting a weight target.

commonTraps: Several options are legitimate behavioural strategies; identify which one tests this particular prediction.
recogniseNextTime: Match the CBT technique to its purpose: monitoring identifies patterns; an experiment tests a prediction.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What should be recorded before the experiment?
followUpQuestions.answer: The predicted outcome, for example how tense the patient expects to feel if they try the alternative response.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: A behavioural experiment tests a specific prediction against experience. Trying another response and comparing expected with actual tension tests whether snacking is necessary for the tension to settle.

questions.stem: A blood film shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Which mechanism most directly produces this combination?
options: Loss of red-cell membrane surface area
Reduced globin-chain synthesis
Mechanical fragmentation of circulating erythrocytes
Impaired DNA synthesis in developing blood cells
Reduced iron availability for haem synthesis
questions.why: The film suggests **megaloblastic erythropoiesis**, commonly caused by B12 or folate deficiency impairing DNA synthesis.
distractors: This can produce spherocytes, not megaloblastic change.
This typically produces a microcytic pattern.
This produces fragments such as schistocytes.
This also tends towards microcytosis rather than macro-ovalocytes.
lo: Describe the appearance of the blood film in commonly occurring anaemias
sources: Macrocytic Anemia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459295/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Anaemia.

explanation: Large oval red cells suggest megaloblastic maturation; reduced globin or iron availability usually produces microcytosis.
The abnormality affects a second blood-cell lineage, supporting impaired DNA synthesis rather than an isolated red-cell membrane or mechanical injury.

keyConcept.summary: The film suggests megaloblastic erythropoiesis, commonly caused by B12 or folate deficiency impairing DNA synthesis.
paragraphs: Cell growth can continue while DNA replication and nuclear maturation are delayed. Macrocytosis alone has many causes; the combination with hypersegmented neutrophils is more informative. B12 and folate status must be distinguished clinically.

commonTraps: Do not treat every high MCV as synonymous with B12 deficiency.
recogniseNextTime: Both erythrocyte and neutrophil changes support impaired nuclear maturation.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why does the neutrophil finding matter?
followUpQuestions.answer: It supports a maturation defect affecting more than the red-cell lineage.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The film suggests megaloblastic erythropoiesis, commonly caused by B12 or folate deficiency impairing DNA synthesis.

questions.stem: An isolated ventricular myocyte is exposed to a drug that reduces calcium entry through L-type channels. Which immediate change best explains the fall in contraction strength?
options: Less calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Greater calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Reduced sensitivity of troponin C to calcium
Reduced binding of ATP to myosin heads
Less calcium binding to calmodulin in the contractile apparatus
questions.why: Incoming calcium triggers **calcium-induced calcium release** from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Less trigger calcium means less calcium available to bind troponin C.
distractors: Enhanced uptake can accelerate relaxation, but it is not the direct consequence asked about.
The main effect is reduced calcium availability, not a direct change in troponin affinity.
L-type calcium blockade does not directly prevent ATP binding to myosin.
Cardiac contraction is regulated chiefly by troponin, unlike smooth muscle.
lo: Describe the features of cardiac muscle and its mechanism of contraction, distinguishing it from skeletal and smooth muscle
sources: OpenStax: Cardiac muscle and electrical activity — https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-2-cardiac-muscle-and-electrical-activity
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Ischaemic Heart Disease).

keyClues.quote: reduces calcium entry through L-type channels
explanation: The entry step is the trigger for a larger intracellular calcium release.

keyConcept.summary: Incoming calcium triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
paragraphs: Cardiac excitation–contraction coupling links the membrane action potential to intracellular calcium. Calcium binding to troponin moves tropomyosin away from actin’s binding sites. Relaxation requires calcium removal from the cytosol.

commonTraps: Do not apply smooth-muscle calmodulin regulation to a ventricular myocyte.
recogniseNextTime: The entry step is the trigger for a larger intracellular calcium release.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why does reduced cytosolic calcium reduce force?
followUpQuestions.answer: Fewer actin–myosin interactions can be activated through the troponin–tropomyosin system.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Incoming calcium triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

questions.stem: A smoker has airflow obstruction, hyperinflation and reduced gas-transfer capacity. Histology shows enlarged airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles with destruction of alveolar walls. Which pathological process best fits?
options: Chronic bronchitis
Emphysema
Lobar pneumonia
Pulmonary fibrosis
Bronchiectasis
questions.why: **Emphysema** destroys alveolar walls, reducing elastic recoil and gas-exchange surface area.
distractors: Mucus hypersecretion and airway changes are central; alveolar-wall destruction defines emphysema.
Alveolar inflammatory exudate causes consolidation rather than this chronic destructive pattern.
Fibrosis thickens and stiffens the interstitium rather than destroying walls into enlarged airspaces.
This involves permanently dilated bronchi, often with chronic infection.
lo: Explain and compare the immunological and pathological changes occurring in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma and how these result in the symptoms and signs of the disease
sources: What do we know about mechanical strain in lung alveoli? - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3213982/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Introduction).

explanation: Air trapping plus reduced transfer suggests loss of effective alveolar surface area. Chronic bronchitis alone does not explain the destructive gas-transfer defect as well.
This is the defining destructive feature of emphysema. Bronchiectasis concerns dilated bronchi, while fibrosis thickens and scars interstitial tissue.

keyConcept.summary: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, reducing elastic recoil and gas-exchange surface area.
paragraphs: Loss of recoil encourages small-airway collapse during expiration and air trapping. Increased compliance is not equivalent to healthier lungs: an easily expanded lung may empty poorly and have less effective surface area.

commonTraps: Do not assume every obstructive smoker has only chronic bronchitis.
recogniseNextTime: Wall loss explains both enlarged airspaces and reduced gas transfer.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why can the chest become hyperinflated?
followUpQuestions.answer: Reduced recoil and expiratory airway collapse trap gas.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, reducing elastic recoil and gas-exchange surface area.

questions.stem: An older adult has lost substantial muscle mass. Serum creatinine remains within the laboratory range despite evidence of reduced renal filtration. Which factor can make creatinine-based estimates overestimate kidney function?
options: Increased creatinine production after a meat-heavy meal
Reduced creatinine generation from muscle
Inhibition of tubular creatinine secretion by a medicine
Increased creatinine generation from muscle injury
Reduced glomerular filtration of creatinine
questions.why: Less muscle can mean **less creatinine production**, so a relatively low concentration may conceal a reduced GFR.
distractors: This can raise the concentration, the opposite direction to the marker limitation described.
This usually raises serum creatinine without a corresponding fall in true GFR.
Muscle breakdown can increase the creatinine load; the stem describes loss of muscle mass.
Reduced filtration tends to raise creatinine rather than explain a deceptively low concentration.
lo: Interpret simple tests of renal function, including plasma creatinine urea and eGFR, explaining the limitations of each
sources: Renal Function Tests - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507821/?report=reader
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Acute Kidney Injury.

explanation: Less muscle generates less creatinine, so the blood concentration can look reassuring despite impaired clearance.

keyClues.quote: within the laboratory range despite evidence of reduced renal filtration
explanation: The task is to explain a deceptively low marker. Reduced filtration or inhibited tubular secretion tends to increase creatinine, rather than explain this discordance.

keyConcept.summary: Less muscle can mean less creatinine production, so a relatively low concentration may conceal a reduced GFR.
paragraphs: A laboratory reference range is not a guarantee of normal organ function in every patient. Creatinine-based estimates assume a relationship between generation and clearance that becomes less reliable at extremes of muscle mass. Alternative assessment may be needed.

commonTraps: Do not interpret “within range” without the patient’s context.
recogniseNextTime: The marker’s production rate has changed as well as its renal clearance.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Does serum creatinine measure GFR directly?
followUpQuestions.answer: No. It is an endogenous marker used to estimate filtration.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Less muscle can mean less creatinine production, so a relatively low concentration may conceal a reduced GFR.

questions.stem: Iron deficiency suppresses hepcidin production. Which change at the basolateral surface of an intestinal enterocyte increases iron delivery to the blood?
options: Increased conversion of iron into haemoglobin inside the enterocyte
Increased internalisation and degradation of ferroportin
Reduced export of iron from intracellular stores
Reduced transferrin synthesis within the enterocyte
Greater persistence of ferroportin on the membrane
questions.why: Low hepcidin permits **ferroportin-mediated iron export** from enterocytes and iron-recycling cells into plasma.
distractors: Enterocytes are not the main site of haemoglobin synthesis.
This is the effect of higher, not lower, hepcidin.
That would reduce iron delivery to the circulation.
Transferrin is chiefly a circulating liver-derived carrier, not this export mechanism.
lo: Explain the processes of digestion, absorption and excretion occurring in the digestive tract, focusing particularly on fats, carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins and iron
sources: StatPearls: Hepcidin — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538257/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Malabsorption).

explanation: Lower hepcidin reduces the signal causing ferroportin internalisation and degradation.
This is the export side of the enterocyte: membrane ferroportin transfers iron towards blood. Reduced export would oppose the requested increase.

keyConcept.summary: Low hepcidin permits ferroportin-mediated iron export from enterocytes and iron-recycling cells into plasma.
paragraphs: Hepcidin links iron availability and inflammatory signals to systemic iron supply. Increased hepcidin can trap iron in storage cells even when total body iron is present, helping explain iron restriction during inflammation.

commonTraps: Do not confuse stored iron with iron available for erythropoiesis.
recogniseNextTime: The question concerns exit towards blood, not uptake from the intestinal lumen.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What does inflammation often do to hepcidin?
followUpQuestions.answer: It increases hepcidin, reducing iron export into plasma.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Low hepcidin permits ferroportin-mediated iron export from enterocytes and iron-recycling cells into plasma.

questions.stem: A child has both 46,XX and 47,XX,+21 cell populations. The embryo initially had a normal 46,XX chromosome complement. Which subsequent event best explains the trisomic cell population?
options: Failure of homologous chromosome 21 separation during maternal meiosis I
Failure of chromosome 21 sister-chromatid separation during maternal meiosis II
Loss of one chromosome 21 by anaphase lag in a trisomic embryonic cell
A balanced Robertsonian fusion involving chromosomes 14 and 21 in an embryonic cell
Failure of chromosome 21 sister-chromatid separation during embryonic mitosis
questions.why: Mitotic nondisjunction in a cell of an initially euploid embryo can produce a trisomic daughter cell. Descendants of unaffected cells retain 46 chromosomes, giving a mosaic pattern.
distractors: Maternal meiosis I occurs before fertilisation. An abnormal gamete would not explain a new trisomic lineage arising from the stated euploid embryo.
Maternal meiosis II is part of gamete formation, not subsequent embryonic cell division.
Trisomy rescue can generate a normal lineage from a trisomic embryo, but the question specifies the reverse starting point.
A balanced Robertsonian fusion rearranges chromosomal material; it does not generate the specified 47-chromosome trisomy.
lo: Using molecular insight outline the clinical implications of chromosomal non-disjunction at meiosis I, meiosis II or mitosis
sources: Down syndrome: MedlinePlus Genetics — https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/down-syndrome/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Congenital Disorders (Down's Syndrome).
NHGRI, Mosaicism — https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Mosaicism

keyClues.quote: initially had a normal 46,XX chromosome complement
explanation: The abnormal lineage must arise after fertilisation from a euploid starting point.
The additional whole chromosome is consistent with segregation failure, not a balanced fusion.

keyConcept.summary: Mitotic nondisjunction in a cell of an initially euploid embryo can produce a trisomic daughter cell. Descendants of unaffected cells retain 46 chromosomes, giving a mosaic pattern.
paragraphs: Use the starting chromosome complement and the timing of cell division to distinguish meiotic from mitotic errors.
Mosaic trisomy can also arise through loss of a chromosome from an initially trisomic embryo. The initial normal complement is specified here so that trisomy rescue is not a second defensible answer.

commonTraps: Mosaicism alone does not prove that the embryo started euploid.
recogniseNextTime: Use the starting chromosome complement and the timing of cell division to distinguish meiotic from mitotic errors.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What does trisomy rescue mean?
followUpQuestions.answer: Loss of an extra chromosome from a trisomic cell, potentially leaving a disomic cell lineage.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Mitotic nondisjunction in a cell of an initially euploid embryo can produce a trisomic daughter cell. Descendants of unaffected cells retain 46 chromosomes, giving a mosaic pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with stable angina starts a selective beta-1 blocker. Which pair of changes most directly reduces myocardial oxygen demand during exercise?
options: Lower heart rate and higher contractility
Higher heart rate and lower contractility
Lower venous tone and lower platelet aggregation
Lower afterload and higher contractility
Lower heart rate and lower contractility
questions.why: Beta-1 blockade reduces **heart rate and contractility**, lowering the work and oxygen demand of the heart.
distractors: The contractility change is opposite to beta-1 blockade.
Beta-1 blockade normally blunts the exercise-related heart-rate rise.
These are more characteristic of nitrates and antiplatelet treatment, respectively.
Increased contractility would increase oxygen demand and is not the direct beta-1 effect.
lo: Explain the mechanism of action of nitrates, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers in the treatment of ischaemic chest pain
sources: Selective Beta-1 Blockers - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499982/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Ischaemic Heart Disease).

explanation: Beta-1 receptors mediate sympathetic increases in cardiac rate and force.

keyConcept.summary: Beta-1 blockade reduces heart rate and contractility, lowering the work and oxygen demand of the heart.
paragraphs: Angina occurs when oxygen supply cannot meet myocardial demand. Slowing the heart can also lengthen diastole, when left ventricular coronary perfusion predominantly occurs. The drug does not remove an atherosclerotic narrowing or dissolve a clot.

commonTraps: Do not select an anti-thrombotic mechanism for a drug acting on cardiac adrenergic receptors.
recogniseNextTime: Beta-1 receptors mediate sympathetic increases in cardiac rate and force.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which receptor mediates most salbutamol bronchodilation?
followUpQuestions.answer: Beta-2 receptors in airway smooth muscle.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Beta-1 blockade reduces heart rate and contractility, lowering the work and oxygen demand of the heart.

questions.stem: A university student develops a gradually worsening dry cough and headache. Imaging shows patchy pneumonia. The organism detected lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall. Which pathogen is most likely?
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Legionella pneumophila
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Haemophilus influenzae
questions.why: **Mycoplasma pneumoniae** lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall and can cause a relatively gradual atypical pneumonia.
distractors: This is a Gram-positive encapsulated diplococcus with a cell wall.
Klebsiella is an encapsulated Gram-negative bacterium with a peptidoglycan-containing cell wall; it does not match the stated structural finding.
This atypical pathogen has a Gram-negative-type cell envelope; it is not wall-less.
This is a small Gram-negative coccobacillus with a cell wall.
lo: Describe the characteristics of Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Mycoplasma pneumoniae; including how they infect patients, and how infection with them is diagnosed and treated
sources: StatPearls: Mycoplasma infections — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK536927/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Infections).
https://www.cdc.gov/mycoplasma/hcp/clinical-care/index.html

keyClues.quote: gradually worsening dry cough and headache
explanation: A gradual respiratory illness is compatible with Mycoplasma, but the symptoms alone do not reliably identify an organism. The cell-wall finding is the discriminating evidence.
Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall. Each of the other four listed bacteria has a peptidoglycan-containing envelope, so this finding separates the options more reliably than the symptom pattern.

keyConcept.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall and can cause a relatively gradual atypical pneumonia.
paragraphs: Symptoms alone overlap between pathogens. Connecting microbial structure with treatment helps: a drug targeting peptidoglycan synthesis has no appropriate target in Mycoplasma. This does not by itself specify the best regimen for every patient.

commonTraps: Atypical pneumonia is a clinical pattern, not a unique organism.
recogniseNextTime: The structural feature discriminates between clinically overlapping causes of atypical pneumonia.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why are beta-lactams ineffective against Mycoplasma?
followUpQuestions.answer: Their cell-wall target is absent.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

editorialRevision.reason: Replace the ambiguous Chlamydia distractor and correct the clue comparison.
editorialRevision.review: AI editorial revision with targeted source checks; not independent clinician sign-off.

questions.assessmentObjective: Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall and can cause a relatively gradual atypical pneumonia.

questions.stem: A young adult has recurrent abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Ileocolonoscopy shows separated inflamed segments. After surgery for a bowel stricture, a resection specimen demonstrates inflammation extending deeply through the bowel wall. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Crohn’s disease
Coeliac disease
Ulcerative colitis
Ischaemic colitis
Microscopic colitis
questions.why: **Skip lesions and transmural inflammation** favour Crohn’s disease over ulcerative colitis.
distractors: This principally affects small-intestinal villi rather than producing transmural skip lesions.
This usually starts in the rectum and extends continuously, with predominantly mucosal inflammation.
Its distribution and acute vascular context differ from the recurrent transmural skip pattern.
This commonly causes watery diarrhoea with a relatively normal endoscopic appearance.
lo: Identify the major distinctions between the pathology and clinical features of ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease
sources: Definition & Facts for Crohn’s Disease - NIDDK — https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/crohns-disease/definition-facts
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Malignancy).
https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/crohns-disease/diagnosis

explanation: Skip lesions favour Crohn’s disease over the usual continuous colonic pattern of ulcerative colitis.

keyClues.quote: inflammation extending deeply through the bowel wall
explanation: Transmural inflammation further supports Crohn’s disease. Coeliac disease primarily affects small-bowel mucosa, and microscopic colitis does not produce this transmural pattern.

keyConcept.summary: Skip lesions and transmural inflammation favour Crohn’s disease over ulcerative colitis.
paragraphs: Transmural disease can lead to strictures, fistulae and abscesses. Ulcerative colitis is usually continuous and confined to the colon. Neither diagnosis is made from one symptom alone; distribution and pathology help distinguish them.

A routine endoscopic biopsy samples the mucosa and cannot establish the full depth of bowel-wall inflammation. A surgical resection specimen includes the full wall and can demonstrate transmural disease.

commonTraps: Do not use diarrhoea alone to distinguish inflammatory bowel diseases.
recogniseNextTime: Patchiness is important when combined with the depth of inflammation.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why are fistulae more associated with Crohn’s?

questions.stem: A biopsy shows malignant epithelial cells occupying the full thickness of an epithelial layer. The basement membrane is intact and there is no stromal invasion. Which term best describes the lesion?
options: Carcinoma in situ
Invasive carcinoma
Simple hyperplasia
Metaplasia
Metastatic carcinoma
questions.why: Malignant epithelium confined above an intact basement membrane is **carcinoma in situ**.
distractors: This requires penetration into the underlying stroma.
Increased cell number alone does not account for malignant cells throughout the epithelial thickness.
This is replacement by another differentiated cell type, without the stated malignant cytology.
Metastasis means spread to a separate site, which is not described.
lo: Explain the terms used to define dysplasia and neoplasia and outline the clinical relevance of each, using these terms to understand the differences between in situ carcinoma from invasive carcinoma
sources: Definition of carcinoma in situ - NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms - NCI — https://www.cancer.gov/publications/dictionaries/cancer-terms/def/carcinoma-in-situ
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Malignancies (Breast Cancer).

keyClues.quote: malignant epithelial cells occupying the full thickness
explanation: The cytological and architectural abnormality is more than simple increased cell number or substitution of one mature cell type for another.
Preservation of this boundary establishes an in-situ lesion; stromal invasion is required for invasive carcinoma.
The described specimen is a local non-invasive epithelial lesion, not a demonstrated metastatic deposit.

keyConcept.summary: Malignant epithelium confined above an intact basement membrane is carcinoma in situ.
paragraphs: Cytological abnormality and anatomical invasion answer different questions. A lesion may be malignant in appearance yet remain confined to its epithelial compartment. The stem explicitly includes malignant cytology, avoiding the false inference that any cells above a basement membrane are carcinoma.

commonTraps: An intact basement membrane alone is not enough; normal epithelium also has one.
recogniseNextTime: The boundary between in situ and invasive carcinoma is invasion through the basement membrane.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What change establishes invasive carcinoma?
followUpQuestions.answer: Tumour cells entering the underlying stroma.

questions.stem: A patient with orthopnoea has a chest X-ray reported as showing cardiomegaly, upper-lobe venous diversion and bilateral perihilar air-space shadowing. Which mechanism best explains the lung findings?
options: Reduced pulmonary capillary pressure after embolism
Increased pleural negative pressure during an obstructed inspiration
Increased alveolar-capillary permeability after aspiration
Increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from nephrotic syndrome
questions.why: Left-sided cardiac failure can raise pulmonary venous and capillary pressure. **Hydrostatic pulmonary oedema** accounts for the vascular redistribution and air-space fluid.
distractors: A fall in capillary pressure does not drive fluid into alveoli.
Negative-pressure oedema is a different acute mechanism, without the chronic cardiac clues here.
This can cause non-cardiogenic oedema but does not best integrate cardiomegaly and venous diversion.
This can contribute to oedema, but the cardiac and vascular distribution points to raised filling pressure.
lo: Identify common tests used to diagnose heart failure, including echocardiography and chest x-ray, relating this to the pathophysiology of the disease
sources: Clinical Methods: Chest roentgenography for pulmonary evaluation — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK370/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

explanation: Breathlessness on lying flat is consistent with pulmonary congestion, but is supportive rather than diagnostic on its own.
These findings support raised pulmonary venous pressure from cardiac dysfunction, making a hydrostatic mechanism more likely than isolated low albumin or aspiration injury.
In combination with the congestion signs, this supports cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Reduced capillary pressure would oppose that fluid movement.

keyConcept.summary: Left-sided cardiac failure can raise pulmonary venous and capillary pressure
paragraphs: Fluid first accumulates in the interstitium and can then enter alveoli. Orthopnoea fits worsening pulmonary congestion when lying flat. A radiology report supports a mechanism but does not replace assessment of symptoms and cardiac function.

commonTraps: Bilateral opacities alone are not specific for cardiac failure; use the accompanying findings.
recogniseNextTime: Venous redistribution supports elevated pulmonary venous pressure rather than isolated airway disease.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why can gas exchange deteriorate?
followUpQuestions.answer: Fluid thickens the diffusion pathway and creates poorly ventilated but perfused lung regions.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.stem: A patient with a left hilar lung tumour develops a hoarse voice. Laryngoscopy shows left vocal-cord paralysis. Which nerve is most likely affected?
options: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve
External branch of the left superior laryngeal nerve
Left hypoglossal nerve
Left phrenic nerve
Right recurrent laryngeal nerve
questions.why: The **left recurrent laryngeal nerve** loops beneath the aortic arch before ascending towards the larynx, making it vulnerable to thoracic disease.
distractors: This supplies cricothyroid and affects pitch; recurrent laryngeal injury better explains vocal-cord paralysis.
This mainly controls tongue movement.
This supplies the diaphragm rather than the intrinsic laryngeal muscles.
This would primarily affect the right vocal cord and has a different thoracic course.
lo: Describe the range of presenting symptoms of lung cancer and explain how they relate to the pathology of the underlying diseases
sources: Embryology, Aortic Arch - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK553173/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Malignancies).

explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve has a thoracic course looping beneath the aortic arch, making it vulnerable to adjacent thoracic disease.
This localises the motor deficit to the left laryngeal supply. Phrenic and hypoglossal lesions affect diaphragm and tongue, while the external superior laryngeal branch chiefly supplies cricothyroid.

keyConcept.summary: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath the aortic arch before ascending towards the larynx, making it vulnerable to thoracic disease.
paragraphs: The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply most intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Their asymmetric courses explain why a left thoracic lesion can cause hoarseness. Phrenic involvement would instead affect diaphragmatic movement.

commonTraps: Do not choose the phrenic nerve simply because the lesion is intrathoracic.
recogniseNextTime: The side and affected structure locate the relevant motor supply.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle has a different motor supply?
followUpQuestions.answer: Cricothyroid, supplied by the external superior laryngeal branch.
