questions.stem: A haemoglobin variant polymerises more readily when deoxygenated, distorting erythrocytes and contributing to vaso-occlusion. Which change causes classical sickle haemoglobin?
options: A complete absence of alpha-globin synthesis
Loss of the red-cell membrane protein spectrin
Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Reduced beta-globin production without the HbS substitution
A glutamate-to-valine substitution in beta globin
questions.why: HbS contains a **beta-globin amino-acid substitution** that promotes polymerisation in the deoxygenated state.
distractors: This describes severe alpha-thalassaemia rather than HbS.
This causes a membrane disorder rather than the HbS structural variant.
This affects oxidative defence, not globin sequence.
This describes beta-thalassaemia.
lo: Describe the genetic basis of the common haemoglobinopathies, including alpha and beta thalassaemia and sickle cell disease
sources: Sickle Cell Disease - GeneReviews® - NCBI Bookshelf — https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1377/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Anaemia.

explanation: Deoxygenation-dependent polymerisation is the central property of HbS, produced by the beta-globin glutamate-to-valine substitution.
Sickling-related loss of deformability explains vascular obstruction; membrane spectrin or G6PD defects cause haemolysis through different mechanisms.

keyConcept.summary: HbS contains a beta-globin amino-acid substitution that promotes polymerisation in the deoxygenated state.
paragraphs: Sickle cell disease and thalassaemia both involve haemoglobin but through different molecular mechanisms: altered structure versus reduced chain synthesis. Genotype influences phenotype, and the two can coexist.

commonTraps: Do not use “reduced haemoglobin production” as the specific HbS mechanism.
recogniseNextTime: The oxygen-dependent structural behaviour identifies HbS rather than a globin-production defect.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What environmental change favours HbS polymerisation?
followUpQuestions.answer: Deoxygenation.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: HbS contains a beta-globin amino-acid substitution that promotes polymerisation in the deoxygenated state.

questions.stem: A service wants to reduce recurrent cardiovascular events in patients with established coronary disease. Which intervention is secondary prevention in this context?
options: Blood-pressure screening in adults without known cardiovascular disease
Reducing dietary salt in a school-meal programme
Smoking-prevention education before tobacco use begins
Statin treatment after a documented myocardial infarction
Screening asymptomatic relatives for cardiovascular risk factors
questions.why: Treatment after established coronary disease aims to prevent **further events**, making it secondary prevention in cardiovascular practice.
distractors: This is primary prevention in the stated context.
This is population-level primary prevention.
This is prevention before disease develops.
This is primary prevention for relatives without established disease.
lo: Distinguish between primary and secondary prevention, giving examples of each
sources: Quality statement 5: Secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease | Cardiovascular risk assessment and lipid modification | Quality standards | NICE — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs100/chapter/Quality-statement-5-Secondary-prevention-of-cardiovascular-disease
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Ischaemic Heart Disease).

explanation: The patient already has the disease; prevention level depends on that starting point.

keyConcept.summary: Treatment after established coronary disease aims to prevent further events, making it secondary prevention in cardiovascular practice.
paragraphs: The same drug can be used for primary or secondary prevention in different people. Terminology also varies by context: in screening theory, secondary prevention often refers to early disease detection. Here the cardiovascular-event context is explicit.

commonTraps: Do not assign prevention level from the drug name alone.
recogniseNextTime: The patient already has the disease; prevention level depends on that starting point.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Can a statin also be used in primary prevention?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes, in someone without established cardiovascular disease when indicated.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Treatment after established coronary disease aims to prevent further events, making it secondary prevention in cardiovascular practice.

questions.stem: After equal intravenous doses of two drugs, the initial equilibrated plasma concentration of X is much lower than that of Y. Assuming negligible elimination during this comparison, what does this suggest?
options: X has a smaller apparent volume of distribution
X has a larger apparent volume of distribution
X must have a shorter elimination half-life
X necessarily has a higher renal clearance
X has a higher oral bioavailability
questions.why: **Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration**. With equal amounts, lower plasma concentration indicates larger apparent Vd.
distractors: For the same amount, a lower concentration implies a larger Vd.
Half-life depends on both distribution volume and clearance.
Elimination is excluded from the comparison and Vd does not specify clearance.
Both doses were intravenous, so oral absorption is irrelevant.
lo: Calculate drug dilutions and doses using volumes of distribution and drug clearances to obtain safe and effective concentrations of drugs in plasma
sources: StatPearls: Pharmacokinetics — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557744/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

explanation: The delivered dose is controlled and there is no oral absorption comparison.

keyClues.quote: plasma concentration of X is much lower
explanation: Apparent volume of distribution equals amount of drug in the body divided by plasma concentration: a lower concentration at the same amount means a larger apparent volume.
Clearance differences are excluded as the explanation during this comparison, and half-life cannot be inferred from concentration alone.

keyConcept.summary: Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration
paragraphs: Apparent Vd is a mathematical volume, not a measured anatomical compartment. Extensive tissue binding can produce values greater than total body volume because plasma contains only a small fraction of the total drug.

commonTraps: Do not infer elimination rate from distribution volume alone.
recogniseNextTime: This isolates distribution from loss of drug from the body.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which dose is directly influenced by Vd?
followUpQuestions.answer: The loading dose for a chosen target concentration.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration

questions.stem: A 28-year-old has recurrent episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations with marked blood-pressure surges. Blood pressure is lower between episodes. Which secondary cause is most likely?
options: Primary hyperaldosteronism
Phaeochromocytoma
Coarctation of the aorta
Renal artery stenosis
Cushing syndrome
questions.why: Episodic catecholamine release from a **phaeochromocytoma** can produce this combination of symptoms and pressure surges.
distractors: This can cause sustained hypertension and hypokalaemia but does not best explain the paroxysmal adrenergic pattern.
This would suggest arm–leg pressure and pulse differences rather than adrenergic attacks.
This activates the renin–angiotensin system but is less characteristic of these episodic symptoms.
This causes a different pattern of systemic features and usually more sustained hypertension.
lo: Identify the risk factors predisposing to high blood pressure, including the causes of secondary hypertension
sources: Episodic palpitations in pheochromocytoma - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2774366/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Hypertension).

explanation: The symptom cluster fits episodic catecholamine excess.
Paroxysms with lower pressure between episodes strengthen the case for phaeochromocytoma over the more sustained hypertension typical of the other listed causes.

keyConcept.summary: Episodic catecholamine release from a phaeochromocytoma can produce this combination of symptoms and pressure surges.
paragraphs: Secondary hypertension should be considered when age, severity or associated features are atypical. The clinical pattern raises suspicion but is not diagnostic without appropriate biochemical and anatomical assessment.

commonTraps: A headache in any hypertensive patient is not sufficient to identify this tumour.
recogniseNextTime: Paroxysmal symptoms are more informative than hypertension alone.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which broad class of mediators is released?
followUpQuestions.answer: Catecholamines.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Episodic catecholamine release from a phaeochromocytoma can produce this combination of symptoms and pressure surges.

questions.stem: A doctor discovers that their signed note incorrectly records a normal neurological examination that was not performed. The patient remains on the ward. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait until the next routine ward round before mentioning the error
Delete the original entry and replace it with a normal examination after seeing the patient
Add the examination to the discharge summary only
Ask a colleague to perform the examination without correcting the note
Make a dated correction preserving the original entry and inform the team so the patient can be reassessed
questions.why: The response should combine **transparent correction and prompt clinical communication**, with reassessment of any unmet need.
distractors: This leaves the team relying on inaccurate information in the meantime.
This obscures what was recorded and when.
A later summary does not correct the immediate clinical record.
Reassessment alone leaves a misleading record.
lo: Be familiar with the principles of good medical practice and the reasoning behind them as defined by the GMC
sources: GMC: Colleagues, culture and safety — https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/the-professional-standards/good-medical-practice/domain-3-colleagues-culture-and-safety
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

explanation: The record contains a factual error; obtaining an examination later cannot make the original entry accurate.
The team can act now to reassess the patient. A traceable correction and communication address both record integrity and current clinical care.

keyConcept.summary: The response should combine transparent correction and prompt clinical communication, with reassessment of any unmet need.
paragraphs: An accurate audit trail helps others understand what was known at each stage. Correcting documentation and addressing patient safety are complementary tasks. Follow local reporting and candour processes where applicable.

commonTraps: Do not erase the history of an error to make the record look cleaner.
recogniseNextTime: The problem is a false record of an assessment, not merely a typographical error.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why inform the clinical team as well as amend the note?
followUpQuestions.answer: They may already be making decisions based on the incorrect information.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The response should combine transparent correction and prompt clinical communication, with reassessment of any unmet need.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient has limited English and is discussing an important non-urgent screening decision. Their adult relative offers to interpret. What is the best next arrangement?
options: Postpone discussion indefinitely until the patient learns more English
Give an English leaflet and proceed if the patient nods
Use the relative by default because they know the patient well
Ask the relative to choose the screening option
Offer a professional interpreter and speak directly to the patient
questions.why: Offer **professional interpretation** so the patient can understand, ask questions and make their own decision.
distractors: This creates an avoidable barrier to informed care.
Nodding does not establish adequate understanding.
This may affect accuracy, privacy and the patient’s freedom to express concerns.
The decision belongs to the patient, not the interpreter.
lo: Discuss the factors which promote or inhibit effective communication with patients and colleagues
sources: NHS England » Interpreting and translation in primary care — https://www.england.nhs.uk/interpreting/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Start in Life.

explanation: There is time to arrange reliable communication so consent can be informed.
A relative may provide support but should not automatically replace a professional interpreter or make the decision for the patient.

keyConcept.summary: Offer professional interpretation so the patient can understand, ask questions and make their own decision.
paragraphs: Address the patient, use manageable sections and check understanding through the interpreter. A relative may provide support if the patient wishes, but support and accurate independent interpretation are different roles.

commonTraps: Fluency of a relative does not automatically make them the best interpreter for a sensitive decision.
recogniseNextTime: There is time to arrange communication support rather than rely on an unsuitable shortcut.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Who should the clinician address?
followUpQuestions.answer: The patient directly.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Offer professional interpretation so the patient can understand, ask questions and make their own decision.

questions.stem: After stoma surgery, a patient avoids intimacy because they fear leakage and their partner’s reaction. Which initial response is most appropriate?
options: Explore both concerns and offer tailored stoma and relationship support
Reassure them that their partner will certainly be accepting
Provide a standard appliance leaflet without discussing intimacy
Refer for treatment of depression without further assessment
Arrange appliance replacement before asking about actual leakage
questions.why: Explore the patient’s **practical and emotional concerns** before selecting support.
distractors: This assumes another person’s response and can dismiss the patient’s uncertainty.
It may help technically but misses the expressed relationship concern.
Avoidance and concern do not by themselves establish depression.
The fear may not reflect equipment failure; clarify the problem first.
lo: Identify and discuss ways in which people and those close to them may react to living with a stoma as part of the surgical treatment for colorectal cancer
sources: Recovering and lifestyle changes after an ileostomy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/ileostomy/recovery/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Malignancy).

explanation: This is a practical concern worth exploring before assuming appliance failure or selecting a replacement.
The relational concern also needs attention. Appliance information alone misses it, and the clinician cannot guarantee the partner’s response.
Explore the specific impact and support needs before inferring a depressive disorder from this behaviour alone.

keyConcept.summary: Explore the patient’s practical and emotional concerns before selecting support.
paragraphs: A stoma can affect body image, confidence and relationships as well as physical care. The patient can choose whether and how to involve a partner. Tailored support is more useful than assuming the feared outcome or diagnosis.

commonTraps: Do not promise an emotional outcome you cannot know.
recogniseNextTime: The problem has two components that should not be reduced to appliance technique alone.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What could specialist stoma support address?
followUpQuestions.answer: Appliance confidence, leakage concerns and practical strategies chosen with the patient.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Explore the patient’s practical and emotional concerns before selecting support.

questions.stem: A council wants an intervention that reaches people who do not attend individual lifestyle appointments. Which option changes the population’s default food environment?
options: Ask high-risk patients to keep food diaries
Offer one-to-one dietary consultations by referral
Reformulate widely sold foods to reduce energy density
Prescribe weight-management medication to eligible patients
Add BMI checks to booked annual reviews
questions.why: **Food reformulation** changes the exposure available across the population, including people who never attend a clinic.
distractors: This is an individual behavioural intervention.
This requires individual attendance rather than changing the default environment.
This targets selected individuals, not the default food supply.
This identifies risk among attendees but does not change food composition.
lo: Discuss the roles of individuals and society in the rising prevalence of obesity and its implications for health and healthcare
sources: Reformulation of food and beverage products for healthier diets: policy brief — https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240039919
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Metabolic Disorders (Obesity).

keyClues.quote: people who do not attend individual lifestyle appointments
explanation: An intervention relying on referral or attendance will miss the population specifically mentioned.
Reformulating widely purchased products changes routine exposure without requiring each person to book an appointment or opt into treatment.

keyConcept.summary: Food reformulation changes the exposure available across the population, including people who never attend a clinic.
paragraphs: Population interventions and individual care are complementary. Their reach can differ by affordability and availability, so distribution of benefit still needs evaluation rather than an assumption that all groups benefit equally.

commonTraps: Population reach does not automatically guarantee equitable impact.
recogniseNextTime: Reach beyond healthcare attendance is the key design requirement.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why assess effects across socioeconomic groups?
followUpQuestions.answer: To check whether benefits reduce or widen inequalities.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Food reformulation changes the exposure available across the population, including people who never attend a clinic.

questions.stem: After a head injury, a patient hypoventilates. Arterial pH is 7.27, PaCO2 8.0 kPa and bicarbonate 27 mmol/L. Which primary disorder best fits?
options: Primary metabolic alkalosis
Primary metabolic acidosis
Chronic fully compensated respiratory acidosis
Primary respiratory alkalosis
Acute respiratory acidosis
questions.why: Acidaemia with raised CO2 and a modest bicarbonate rise supports **acute respiratory acidosis** from hypoventilation.
distractors: That would have an increased bicarbonate driving alkalemia rather than this pattern.
The bicarbonate is not reduced as the primary disturbance.
The pH is still low and bicarbonate has not risen to the degree expected after sustained compensation.
This requires reduced CO2, not hypercapnia.
lo: Explain how serious injury may result in abnormal blood gases, and how measurement of these may assist management
sources: StatPearls: Acid base balance — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507807/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Seriously Injured Patient.

explanation: There is acidaemia, so a primary alkalosis does not fit the direction of the pH.
Raised CO2 provides the respiratory acid load and fits the stated hypoventilation.
There is only a small bicarbonate elevation. Markedly low pH with limited compensation fits an acute respiratory acidosis rather than the listed fully compensated chronic state.

keyConcept.summary: Acidaemia with raised CO2 and a modest bicarbonate rise supports acute respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation.
paragraphs: The values are internally consistent: 8.0 kPa is about 60 mmHg, and the Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship gives pH about 7.28. Renal compensation takes longer than immediate buffering.

commonTraps: Do not call a partly buffered acute disorder fully compensated.
recogniseNextTime: CO2 is the primary acidifying change; the bicarbonate is not the cause of acidaemia.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What happens to pH if ventilation restores CO2 towards normal?
followUpQuestions.answer: It rises towards normal, assuming no additional disorder.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Acidaemia with raised CO2 and a modest bicarbonate rise supports acute respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation.

questions.stem: A patient develops dry mouth and difficulty passing urine after starting atropine. Which receptor action explains this combination?
options: Dopamine D2 receptor blockade
Alpha-1 receptor blockade
Beta-1 receptor blockade
Nicotinic neuromuscular receptor blockade
Muscarinic receptor blockade
questions.why: **Muscarinic blockade** reduces parasympathetic salivary secretion and impairs normal bladder emptying.
distractors: This does not best explain the paired peripheral antimuscarinic effects.
This tends to relax the bladder outlet rather than explain retention with dry mouth.
This mainly affects cardiac rate and force.
This would chiefly impair skeletal-muscle transmission.
lo: Explain how drugs can act therapeutically and can produce unwanted effects by mimicking or blocking functions of the autonomic nervous system
sources: Physiology, Muscarinic Receptor - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK555909/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Metabolic Disorders (Diabetes).

explanation: Reduced muscarinic stimulation of salivary secretion explains this symptom.
Muscarinic blockade reduces detrusor contraction and can promote retention. Alpha-1 blockade generally reduces outlet resistance rather than explaining this combination.

keyConcept.summary: Muscarinic blockade reduces parasympathetic salivary secretion and impairs normal bladder emptying.
paragraphs: Autonomic drugs can affect several organs because receptors are distributed widely. Recognising a cluster of adverse effects is more useful than memorising each symptom in isolation.

commonTraps: Do not equate every cholinergic receptor with a nicotinic receptor.
recogniseNextTime: The paired autonomic effects point to a shared receptor class.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What pupil effect can muscarinic blockade produce?
followUpQuestions.answer: Mydriasis, with impaired accommodation.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Muscarinic blockade reduces parasympathetic salivary secretion and impairs normal bladder emptying.

questions.stem: A histological section shows striated muscle fibres with branching cells and intercalated discs. Which tissue is being examined?
options: Skeletal muscle
Peripheral nerve
Smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
questions.why: Striations with branching cells and **intercalated discs** identify cardiac muscle.
distractors: This is striated but has long unbranched multinucleate fibres without intercalated discs.
This contains axons and supporting cells, not the stated muscle architecture.
This lacks visible striations and intercalated discs.
This has aligned collagen bundles rather than contractile striated cells.
lo: Describe the structure and function of the four primary tissue types in the body (connective, epithelial, muscular & neural)
sources: Histology, Heart - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545143/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

explanation: Striations indicate organised sarcomeres and weigh against smooth muscle, nerve and dense connective tissue.
These identify cardiac muscle rather than the long unbranched fibres of skeletal muscle.

keyConcept.summary: Striations with branching cells and intercalated discs identify cardiac muscle.
paragraphs: Intercalated discs combine mechanical attachment and electrical communication, helping myocardium contract as coordinated tissue. Histological identification links structure to function rather than relying on striations alone.

questions.stem: After vaccination, a later encounter with the same antigen produces a faster, stronger response than the first encounter. Which feature best explains this?
options: Antigen-specific memory lymphocytes
Persistently elevated nonspecific complement alone
Increased skin thickness at the vaccination site
Continuous replication of antibody proteins
Permanent activation of every naive lymphocyte
questions.why: Memory B and T cells established after antigen exposure support a more rapid secondary response.
distractors: Complement alone does not explain antigen-specific recall.
A local structural change does not explain a stronger systemic response to the same antigen.
Antibody proteins are synthesised by cells and do not replicate.
Memory involves selected antigen-specific populations, not every naive lymphocyte.
lo: Outline the principles of immunisation and the factors influencing its effectiveness
sources: BM4 Year 1: Respiratory (Infections) - LOs.txt
https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-4-the-adaptive-immune-response-b-lymphocytes-and-antibodies

explanation: Immunological memory is specific. Prior unrelated exposure does not guarantee the same enhanced response.
Previously generated memory cells respond efficiently. This differs from an entirely naive primary response.

paragraphs: Memory B and T cells established after antigen exposure support a more rapid secondary response.
Vaccination trains adaptive responses without requiring natural disease.

commonTraps: Do not attribute adaptive memory to self-replicating antibody.

questions.stem: Left ventricular pressure has just fallen below aortic pressure, but remains above left atrial pressure. Which valve state is expected during this phase?
options: Aortic open and mitral closed
Aortic closed and mitral open
Aortic partly open and mitral open
Aortic open and mitral open
Aortic closed and mitral closed
questions.why: This is **isovolumetric relaxation**: the aortic valve has closed, but the mitral valve has not yet opened.
distractors: The aortic valve closes when ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure.
The mitral valve opens only once ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
The pressure relations favour closure of both valves, not filling.
Normal pressure-driven valve operation does not produce this state here.
lo: Describe the events of the cardiac cycle
sources: The Cardiac Cycle and the Physiological Basis of Left Ventricular Contraction, Ejection, Relaxation, and Filling - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2390899/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Hypertension).

explanation: The adverse pressure gradient closes the aortic valve.
Ventricular pressure is still too high for the mitral valve to open. Both valves are closed during isovolumetric relaxation.

keyConcept.summary: This is isovolumetric relaxation: the aortic valve has closed, but the mitral valve has not yet opened.
paragraphs: Valve movement follows pressure gradients. During the interval with both valves closed, ventricular pressure changes while volume is approximately constant. Use the gradients rather than memorising valve states in isolation.

commonTraps: Do not equate ventricular relaxation with immediate ventricular filling.
recogniseNextTime: Ventricular pressure is still too high for passive inflow from the atrium.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What pressure change starts filling?
followUpQuestions.answer: Ventricular pressure falling below left atrial pressure.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: This is isovolumetric relaxation: the aortic valve has closed, but the mitral valve has not yet opened.

questions.stem: A patient with eosinophilic allergic asthma has a late inflammatory response several hours after exposure. Which cytokine is most directly associated with eosinophil development and survival?
options: IL-10
Interferon-gamma
IL-2
IL-5
IL-17
questions.why: **IL-5** supports eosinophil development, activation and survival in type 2 inflammation.
distractors: This commonly contributes to immune regulation rather than defining eosinophil development.
This is associated especially with TH1 and macrophage activation.
This is important in T-cell proliferation rather than the specific eosinophil link.
This is linked to neutrophil-associated responses.
lo: Explain and compare the immunological and pathological changes occurring in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma and how these result in the symptoms and signs of the disease
sources: Clinical Remission Criteria and Serum Levels of Type 2 Inflammation Mediators during 24 Weeks of Treatment with the Anti-IL-5 Drug Mepolizumab in Patients with T2-High Severe Asthma - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11240777/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Introduction).

explanation: The named effector cell guides the cytokine association.

keyConcept.summary: IL-5 supports eosinophil development, activation and survival in type 2 inflammation.
paragraphs: An early mast-cell response and a later eosinophilic response can occur in the same allergic disease. Distinguish initiation of immediate bronchospasm from maintenance of later inflammation.

commonTraps: Do not substitute IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 as if their main roles were identical.
recogniseNextTime: The named effector cell guides the cytokine association.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which antibody class is central to immediate allergic sensitisation?
followUpQuestions.answer: IgE.

questions.stem: The afferent arteriole constricts while other determinants of filtration are initially unchanged. What happens to glomerular capillary pressure and GFR?
options: Both remain unchanged
Pressure increases while GFR decreases
Both increase
Both decrease
Pressure decreases while GFR increases
questions.why: Afferent constriction reduces blood entering the glomerulus, lowering **glomerular pressure and GFR**.
distractors: The afferent arteriole is a regulator of glomerular haemodynamics.
This is not the direct consequence of reduced afferent inflow.
Afferent constriction reduces inflow and glomerular pressure.
With other determinants unchanged, lower filtration pressure reduces GFR.
lo: Explain the concepts of net filtration pressure and glomerular filtration rate and how these are regulated
sources: Physiology, Renal - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538339/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Acute Kidney Injury.

explanation: The affected vessel is before the glomerular capillary bed.

keyConcept.summary: Afferent constriction reduces blood entering the glomerulus, lowering glomerular pressure and GFR.
paragraphs: Afferent and efferent changes are not interchangeable. The net effect of efferent constriction becomes more complex at high degrees of constriction, so locate the resistance change before applying a simple rule.

commonTraps: Do not reverse afferent and efferent effects.
recogniseNextTime: The affected vessel is before the glomerular capillary bed.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which vessel carries blood away from the glomerulus?
followUpQuestions.answer: The efferent arteriole.

questions.stem: A jaundiced patient has pale stools and a much larger rise in ALP and GGT than in ALT. Which biochemical pattern is most likely?
options: Isolated haemolysis
Predominantly hepatocellular injury
Isolated bone disease
Cholestatic injury or obstruction
Gilbert syndrome
questions.why: A disproportionate **ALP and GGT rise** with pale stools supports cholestasis.
distractors: This mainly increases unconjugated bilirubin and does not best explain raised cholestatic enzymes with pale stools.
This generally has a more prominent aminotransferase rise.
Bone can raise ALP, but the GGT and biliary symptoms support a hepatic source.
This gives isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia rather than the stated enzyme pattern.
lo: Interpret the results of liver function tests, distinguishing between haemolytic jaundice, hepatocellular liver disease and large duct obstruction
sources: Alkaline Phosphatase and Gamma Glutamyltransferase - Clinical Methods - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK203/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Hepatobiliary).

explanation: Reduced bile pigment reaching the bowel supports impaired biliary delivery.

keyClues.quote: much larger rise in ALP and GGT than in ALT
explanation: A disproportionate ALP/GGT rise is cholestatic. GGT supports a hepatobiliary source of ALP rather than isolated bone disease.

keyConcept.summary: A disproportionate ALP and GGT rise with pale stools supports cholestasis.
paragraphs: Cholestasis can be intrahepatic or extrahepatic; the pattern does not identify the site or cause by itself. Further assessment and imaging may be needed. GGT helps contextualise an ALP rise because ALP also comes from bone.

commonTraps: Do not equate every cholestatic pattern with a common-bile-duct stone.
recogniseNextTime: Relative enzyme pattern matters more than simply calling all liver tests abnormal.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why can stools become pale?
followUpQuestions.answer: Less bile pigment reaches the intestine.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: A disproportionate ALP and GGT rise with pale stools supports cholestasis.

questions.stem: A diabetes medicine binds SUR1 on pancreatic beta cells and closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels. Which class is it?
options: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor
Biguanide
GLP-1 receptor agonist
SGLT2 inhibitor
Sulfonylurea
questions.why: **Sulfonylureas** close beta-cell KATP channels, causing depolarisation and calcium-dependent insulin release.
distractors: This delays intestinal carbohydrate digestion.
Metformin does not directly stimulate insulin release through SUR1.
This acts through incretin signalling rather than directly binding SUR1.
This acts on proximal tubular glucose transport.
lo: Understand the mechanism of action of commonly used antidiabetic medications.
sources: StatPearls: Sulfonylureas — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513225/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Metabolic Disorders (Diabetes).

explanation: The binding site discriminates from other medicines that can also affect insulin secretion indirectly.

keyConcept.summary: Sulfonylureas close beta-cell KATP channels, causing depolarisation and calcium-dependent insulin release.
paragraphs: Potassium-channel closure reduces potassium efflux. Depolarisation opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and calcium triggers granule release. Link the steps in order rather than memorising “more insulin” alone.

commonTraps: Do not describe potassium-channel closure as hyperpolarisation.
recogniseNextTime: The binding site discriminates from other medicines that can also affect insulin secretion indirectly.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What immediately follows beta-cell depolarisation?
followUpQuestions.answer: Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Sulfonylureas close beta-cell KATP channels, causing depolarisation and calcium-dependent insulin release.

questions.stem: Two adults have the same BMI, but one has a substantially larger waist circumference. What additional information does the waist measure mainly provide?
options: A direct measurement of total body fat percentage
A direct measurement of skeletal-muscle mass
Distribution of central adiposity
A definitive diagnosis of insulin resistance
A measurement of resting metabolic rate
questions.why: Waist measurement adds information about **central fat distribution** that BMI alone does not capture.
distractors: Waist circumference is not a direct body-composition measurement.
It does not isolate muscle from other tissue.
Central adiposity is associated with risk but does not prove the diagnosis.
This requires a different assessment.
lo: Discuss and compare the measures used to define and assess obesity in the population and in the individual including the body mass index (BMI) and the waist-hip ratio
sources: Identifying and assessing overweight, obesity and central adiposity | Overweight and obesity management | Guidance | NICE — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246/chapter/Identifying-and-assessing-overweight-obesity-and-central-adiposity
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Metabolic Disorders (Obesity).

explanation: Equal mass relative to height does not imply identical fat distribution.

keyConcept.summary: Waist measurement adds information about central fat distribution that BMI alone does not capture.
paragraphs: Anthropometric measures are proxies with limitations. Interpretation depends on the person and appropriate reference criteria. A measure can improve risk assessment without directly measuring every relevant biological process.

commonTraps: Do not treat a risk marker as a definitive metabolic diagnosis.
recogniseNextTime: Equal mass relative to height does not imply identical fat distribution.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What basic limitation does BMI have?
followUpQuestions.answer: It does not distinguish fat mass from lean mass or describe distribution.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Waist measurement adds information about central fat distribution that BMI alone does not capture.

questions.stem: A treatment trial measures the primary outcome in 65% of the intervention group and 95% of controls. Missingness is associated with adverse effects and poorer prognosis. What is the main concern?
options: Ecological fallacy
Recall bias
Bias due to missing outcome data
Length-time bias
Lead-time bias
questions.why: **Differential, prognosis-related missing outcomes** can distort the treatment comparison.
distractors: The analysis is not inferring individual effects from group-level associations.
The problem is absent outcomes, not differential memory.
No screening selection of slower disease is described.
No earlier diagnosis is changing the survival clock.
lo: Describe challenges to internal validity for a randomised controlled trial
sources: Cochrane Handbook: Risk of bias in a randomised trial — https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-08
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

keyClues.quote: 65% of the intervention group and 95% of controls
explanation: Outcome completeness differs between the treatment groups; the analysed sample may no longer preserve the original comparison.

keyClues.quote: Missingness is associated with adverse effects and poorer prognosis
explanation: The missing outcomes are related to likely results. This is informative attrition, not an error in remembering past exposure or a screening-related survival artefact.

keyConcept.summary: Differential, prognosis-related missing outcomes can distort the treatment comparison.
paragraphs: Stopping a drug and losing outcome follow-up are not the same event. Intention-to-treat principles do not magically supply unmeasured outcomes; missing-data assumptions and sensitivity analyses still matter.

commonTraps: Do not claim attrition bias merely because patients discontinue medication if their outcomes remain measured.
recogniseNextTime: The missing participants may differ systematically from those analysed.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Would equal missing percentages guarantee no bias?
followUpQuestions.answer: No; the reasons and relationship to outcomes also matter.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Differential, prognosis-related missing outcomes can distort the treatment comparison.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy in a patient with longstanding hypertension shows homogeneous pink thickening of arteriolar walls with luminal narrowing. Which lesion best fits?
options: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
Medial calcific sclerosis
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
Atherosclerosis
Fibrinoid necrosis
questions.why: **Hyaline arteriolosclerosis** is associated with chronic hypertension and diabetes and narrows small-vessel lumina.
distractors: This produces concentric laminated “onion-skin” thickening rather than homogeneous hyaline material.
This involves calcification of muscular arterial media rather than hyaline arteriolar thickening.
This principally affects larger arteries with intimal plaques, not this arteriolar lesion.
This is destructive acute vascular injury rather than the chronic homogeneous wall change.
lo: Outline the pathological changes occurring in small vessels in hypertension including accelerated hypertension
sources: Pathology of small blood vessel disease in hypertension. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2581443/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Hypertension).

keyClues.quote: homogeneous pink thickening of arteriolar walls
explanation: Hyaline material in small arterial walls is the central morphological clue. Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis instead gives concentric onion-skin layering.
Narrowing accompanies the hyaline wall lesion; this is not merely medial calcification of a larger artery. Atherosclerotic plaques also concern a different vessel-wall pattern.
Chronic pressure injury fits hyaline arteriolosclerosis; fibrinoid necrosis implies a different, more destructive vascular lesion.

keyConcept.summary: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is associated with chronic hypertension and diabetes and narrows small-vessel lumina.
paragraphs: Vascular disease terminology depends on vessel size and layer as well as appearance. Arteriolar narrowing can impair downstream perfusion. Atherosclerosis is related vascular pathology but is not the same microscopic lesion.

commonTraps: Do not call every thickened vessel wall an atherosclerotic plaque.
recogniseNextTime: The morphology distinguishes hyaline from laminated hyperplastic change.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which lesion has an onion-skin appearance?
followUpQuestions.answer: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is associated with chronic hypertension and diabetes and narrows small-vessel lumina.

questions.stem: Pulmonary fibrosis thickens the alveolar-capillary barrier. Holding area and the gas pressure gradient constant, what is the effect on gas diffusion?
options: Diffusion stops only if the airway is completely obstructed
Diffusion is unchanged because only perfusion matters
Diffusion increases as barrier thickness increases
Diffusion increases because surface area must increase
Diffusion decreases as barrier thickness increases
questions.why: Fick’s principle predicts that diffusion varies **inversely with barrier thickness** when other factors are fixed.
distractors: Gas transfer can be impaired without airway obstruction.
Barrier properties also influence diffusion.
This reverses the inverse relationship with diffusion distance.
The stem holds area constant.
lo: Explain how oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged in the lungs, carried in the blood and exchanged in the tissues
sources: Diffusing Capacity of the Lungs for Carbon Monoxide - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK556149/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Introduction).

explanation: Fick’s law makes diffusion inversely related to diffusion distance.

keyClues.quote: Holding area and the gas pressure gradient constant
explanation: The stem isolates thickness; an assumed increase in surface area cannot compensate, and complete airway obstruction is not required.

keyConcept.summary: Fick’s principle predicts that diffusion varies inversely with barrier thickness when other factors are fixed.
paragraphs: Surface area, gradient and membrane properties all matter. Fibrosis can affect several simultaneously in real patients; holding variables constant isolates the tested mechanism.

commonTraps: Do not replace a diffusion problem with an airway-flow explanation.
recogniseNextTime: Only diffusion distance is changed in this comparison.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What effect would reduced surface area have?
followUpQuestions.answer: It would also reduce diffusion.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Fick’s principle predicts that diffusion varies inversely with barrier thickness when other factors are fixed.

questions.stem: Advanced kidney disease reduces net acid excretion. Which lost process most directly contributes to a metabolic acidosis?
options: Pulmonary CO2 elimination
Hydrogen-ion secretion by gastric parietal cells
Excretion of filtered bicarbonate
Release of bicarbonate from pancreatic ducts
Ammonium excretion and generation of new bicarbonate
questions.why: Reduced renal **net acid excretion and bicarbonate regeneration** allow non-volatile acid to accumulate.
distractors: This is a respiratory function; the primary loss in the stem is renal.
This is gastrointestinal secretion rather than a lost renal function.
Losing less bicarbonate would not explain net acid retention.
This is not a renal mechanism of systemic net acid excretion.
lo: Explain the control of acid-base balance and the consequences of this for chronic kidney disease
sources: StatPearls: Acid base balance — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507807/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Acute Kidney Injury.

explanation: The primary problem is metabolic acid handling rather than CO2 elimination.

keyConcept.summary: Reduced renal net acid excretion and bicarbonate regeneration allow non-volatile acid to accumulate.
paragraphs: The kidneys reclaim filtered bicarbonate and generate new bicarbonate while excreting acid, including as ammonium. These are related but distinct tasks. Compensation by increased ventilation can reduce CO2 without restoring the missing renal capacity.

commonTraps: Do not describe respiratory compensation as correction of the renal cause.
recogniseNextTime: The primary problem is metabolic acid handling rather than CO2 elimination.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What direction of CO2 change is expected as respiratory compensation?
followUpQuestions.answer: A fall through increased ventilation.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Reduced renal net acid excretion and bicarbonate regeneration allow non-volatile acid to accumulate.

questions.stem: A hypothetical drug is mainly cleared by hepatic metabolism. Severe liver dysfunction reduces its clearance while the intravenous maintenance dose rate stays unchanged. Under linear kinetics, what is expected at steady state?
options: A lower plasma drug concentration
No concentration change because intravenous drugs bypass the liver
A necessarily shorter elimination half-life
A higher plasma drug concentration
A necessarily smaller volume of distribution
questions.why: With input unchanged, reduced clearance produces a **higher steady-state concentration**.
distractors: Reduced clearance at the same input increases exposure.
IV administration bypasses absorption and first pass, not later hepatic clearance.
Reduced clearance tends to lengthen half-life if Vd is unchanged.
Clearance does not uniquely determine distribution volume.
lo: Explain the functions of the liver in relation to the metabolism of drugs and alcohol
sources: StatPearls: Pharmacokinetics — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557744/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Hepatobiliary).

explanation: Less drug is eliminated per unit concentration.
For linear kinetics, steady-state concentration equals input rate divided by clearance, so concentration rises when clearance falls.
No change in volume of distribution is supplied. A lower clearance does not necessarily shorten half-life or make distribution volume smaller.

keyConcept.summary: With input unchanged, reduced clearance produces a higher steady-state concentration.
paragraphs: Intravenous delivery avoids presystemic loss but does not avoid later metabolism. Real liver disease can also change protein binding and distribution; the stem isolates clearance to make the prediction specific.

commonTraps: Do not confuse first-pass metabolism with all hepatic metabolism.
recogniseNextTime: The balance changes because elimination capacity falls while input is maintained.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If Vd is unchanged, what happens to half-life?
followUpQuestions.answer: It increases as clearance falls.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: With input unchanged, reduced clearance produces a higher steady-state concentration.

questions.stem: A patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor develops genital candidiasis. Which expected drug effect most directly contributes?
options: Increased glucose in urine
Reduced pancreatic insulin secretion to zero
Increased intestinal glucose absorption
Reduced renal blood flow as the primary effect
Direct inhibition of T-cell calcineurin
questions.why: SGLT2 inhibition reduces glucose reabsorption, producing **glycosuria** that can favour genital fungal growth.
distractors: SGLT2 inhibitors do not abolish insulin secretion.
The principal target is renal glucose reabsorption.
This does not explain the local glucose-rich environment.
This is a different immunosuppressive mechanism.
lo: Understand the mechanism of action of commonly used antidiabetic medications.
sources: StatPearls: SGLT2 inhibitors — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK576405/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Metabolic Disorders (Diabetes).

explanation: The renal transporter mechanism links the intended glucose-lowering action to this adverse effect.

keyConcept.summary: SGLT2 inhibition reduces glucose reabsorption, producing glycosuria that can favour genital fungal growth.
paragraphs: A mechanism-based adverse effect is easier to remember than an isolated list. This does not mean every urinary symptom is fungal infection or that the drug directly suppresses immunity; symptoms need appropriate assessment.

commonTraps: Do not classify SGLT2 inhibitors as direct immunosuppressants.
recogniseNextTime: The renal transporter mechanism links the intended glucose-lowering action to this adverse effect.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Where is most SGLT2-mediated glucose reabsorption located?
followUpQuestions.answer: The proximal tubule.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: SGLT2 inhibition reduces glucose reabsorption, producing glycosuria that can favour genital fungal growth.

questions.stem: A patient takes a non-haem oral iron dose with tea. Which interaction can reduce iron absorption?
options: Reduced gastric acid secretion preventing iron solubilisation
Reduced iron release from enterocytes due to increased hepcidin
Competition between calcium and iron during absorption
Reduced conversion of ferric to ferrous iron due to vitamin C deficiency
Binding of iron by dietary polyphenols
questions.why: Tea polyphenols can reduce **non-haem iron availability for absorption**.
distractors: Reduced acidity can impair absorption, but is not the principal direct tea–iron interaction.
This is an important systemic regulatory mechanism, but not the direct luminal interaction with tea.
Calcium can affect iron absorption, but does not identify the relevant tea constituent.
Vitamin C can enhance absorption, but deficiency is not established by taking this dose with tea.
lo: Explain the processes of digestion, absorption and excretion occurring in the digestive tract, focusing particularly on fats, carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins and iron
sources: StatPearls: Iron absorption — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448204/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Malabsorption).

explanation: Non-haem absorption is particularly sensitive to luminal dietary interactions; this asks about the ingested dose.
Tea polyphenols can bind iron and reduce its availability. The stem does not establish vitamin C deficiency, a calcium load or a hepcidin-driven systemic change.

keyConcept.summary: Tea polyphenols can reduce non-haem iron availability for absorption.
paragraphs: Dietary context influences non-haem iron absorption. Haem iron is handled differently, and the whole clinical plan matters more than a single food rule. The question tests an interaction, not an instruction to avoid all tea permanently.

commonTraps: Do not confuse iron absorption with intrinsic-factor-dependent B12 absorption.
recogniseNextTime: The form of iron and the co-ingested drink are the relevant features.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which vitamin can enhance non-haem iron absorption?
followUpQuestions.answer: Vitamin C.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Tea polyphenols can reduce non-haem iron availability for absorption.

questions.stem: Early after a viral infection, a nucleic-acid test is positive but an antibody test is negative. Which explanation best fits?
options: A negative antibody test excludes any current infection
The virus has been eliminated because the antibody result is negative
Nucleic-acid tests directly measure the patient’s antibody concentration
Viral genetic material is detectable before seroconversion
Antibodies must always appear before viral replication
questions.why: The tests measure different targets. **Viral nucleic acid can be detected before antibodies become measurable**.
distractors: This ignores the early diagnostic window.
The positive nucleic-acid result does not support that inference.
They detect nucleic acid rather than antibodies.
The host antibody response takes time to develop.
lo: Discuss the different mechanisms of viral replication and the implications that these have for viral transmission, identification, and control
sources: Interim Guidelines for COVID-19 Antibody Testing | CDC — https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/hcp/testing/antibody-tests-guidelines.html
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Hepatobiliary).

explanation: An adaptive antibody response may not yet be detectable in the early window.

keyClues.quote: a nucleic-acid test is positive but an antibody test is negative
explanation: The tests measure different targets. Detectable viral genetic material can precede seroconversion; a negative antibody result does not establish viral clearance.

paragraphs: Test interpretation depends on the assay, specimen and clinical timing. Detection of nucleic acid does not always prove viable transmissible virus, particularly later in illness, but early antibody negativity does not exclude infection.

commonTraps: Do not interpret a negative antibody result without the window period.
recogniseNextTime: Timing explains the discordance without requiring one test to be wrong.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What does seroconversion mean?
followUpQuestions.answer: Development of detectable antibodies in the blood.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.stem: Several days after myocardial infarction, necrotic tissue is being cleared before collagen-rich scar formation. Which cell population is central to removal of the dead tissue?
options: Plasma cells
Macrophages
Neutrophils
Eosinophils
Fibroblasts
questions.why: **Macrophages** remove necrotic debris during the transition from acute inflammation towards repair.
distractors: These secrete antibodies and are not the principal cells removing infarct debris.
These dominate the early acute inflammatory response, before the macrophage clearance phase.
These are more associated with allergy and parasites than routine infarct clearance.
These contribute matrix and scar formation rather than being the main phagocytic clearance cells.
lo: Describe the typical pathological changes in myocardial infarction at both macroscopic and microscopic levels over time
sources: The cardiac wound healing response to myocardial infarction - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10077990/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Ischaemic Heart Disease).

explanation: The process has moved beyond the earliest acute neutrophil-dominant phase towards macrophage clearance.

keyClues.quote: necrotic tissue is being cleared before collagen-rich scar formation
explanation: Macrophages remove cellular debris. Fibroblasts are important in repair and collagen deposition rather than being the main dead-tissue-clearing population.

keyConcept.summary: Macrophages remove necrotic debris during the transition from acute inflammation towards repair.
paragraphs: Inflammation and healing overlap. The damaged wall can be mechanically vulnerable while dead tissue is removed and before a strong scar forms. Timing is approximate and varies with infarct size and treatment.

commonTraps: Do not expect sharply separated cellular phases in every specimen.
recogniseNextTime: The sequence places the tissue in the clearance phase rather than mature repair.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which cells subsequently contribute much of the scar matrix?
followUpQuestions.answer: Fibroblasts.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Macrophages remove necrotic debris during the transition from acute inflammation towards repair.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic ventilatory impairment receives supplemental oxygen. Saturation rises to 96%, but they become drowsy. Which test most directly assesses possible CO2 retention?
options: Peak expiratory flow alone
Chest radiography alone
Arterial blood gas analysis
Repeat pulse oximetry alone
Serum bicarbonate alone
questions.why: An **arterial blood gas** assesses PaCO2 and pH as well as oxygenation. A satisfactory saturation does not establish adequate ventilation.
distractors: This measures expiratory flow rather than CO2 retention.
This may identify causes but does not measure PaCO2.
Saturation does not measure arterial CO2 or pH.
This may suggest compensation but does not directly establish the current CO2 and pH.
lo: Describe the physiological changes occurring in oxygen therapy, and how these guide management of patients
sources: NICE NG115: COPD recommendations — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115/chapter/Recommendations
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Failures).

explanation: Pulse oximetry reports oxygenation, not ventilation or arterial CO2. A reassuring saturation cannot exclude hypercapnia.
In a patient with ventilatory impairment this warrants assessment for CO2 retention, although drowsiness has other causes.

keyClues.quote: most directly assesses possible CO2 retention
explanation: An arterial gas measures PaCO2 and pH directly; bicarbonate alone, peak flow and an X-ray cannot provide that measurement.

keyConcept.summary: An arterial blood gas assesses PaCO2 and pH as well as oxygenation
paragraphs: Oxygenation and ventilation are related but distinct. In a deteriorating patient, assess promptly and interpret gases alongside the clinical picture; do not assume oxygen should simply be stopped because hypercapnia is possible.

commonTraps: Do not use a normal saturation as proof that CO2 is normal.
recogniseNextTime: Improved oxygenation can coexist with worsening CO2 retention.

questions.stem: During haemodialysis, urea concentration is higher in blood than in fresh dialysate. Which process principally removes this small solute across the membrane?
options: Osmosis of urea molecules
Diffusion down its concentration gradient
ATP-dependent active transport
Endocytosis into dialysis tubing
Binding to erythrocyte surface receptors
questions.why: Urea moves by **diffusion** from higher to lower concentration across the permeable membrane.
distractors: Osmosis refers to solvent movement, not the named solute’s diffusion.
The dialysis membrane does not use ATP to pump urea.
Vesicular cellular uptake is not the mechanism.
This does not explain movement into dialysate.
lo: Outline the principles of haemodialysis and continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis in the management of renal failure
sources: Hemodialysis - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK563296/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Chronic Kidney Injury.

keyClues.quote: higher in blood than in fresh dialysate
explanation: The concentration difference supplies the driving force.

keyConcept.summary: Urea moves by diffusion from higher to lower concentration across the permeable membrane.
paragraphs: Fresh dialysate maintains a favourable gradient. Water removal by pressure-driven ultrafiltration is a separate process, although convection can also carry solute. Distinguish what is moving and which gradient drives it.

commonTraps: Do not use osmosis as a synonym for all movement through a membrane.
recogniseNextTime: The concentration difference supplies the driving force.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What happens if blood and dialysate concentrations become equal?
followUpQuestions.answer: Net diffusive transfer of that solute approaches zero.

questions.stem: A patient has persistent right upper-quadrant pain, fever and inspiratory arrest during palpation beneath the right costal margin. Ultrasound shows gallstones, a thickened gallbladder wall and surrounding fluid, without common-duct dilatation. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Acute cholecystitis
Ascending cholangitis
Viral hepatitis
Acute pancreatitis
Uncomplicated biliary colic
questions.why: Persistent pain with fever and inflammatory gallbladder changes supports **acute cholecystitis**.
distractors: This involves infected obstructed ducts and is less consistent with the isolated gallbladder findings.
This does not best explain the focal inflammatory gallbladder pattern.
This more often has epigastric pain and pancreatic biochemical or imaging findings.
This typically causes transient pain without sustained inflammatory signs or the stated wall changes.
lo: Explain the functions of the gallbladder, and how this may be affected by the presence of gallstones
sources: Prospective evaluation of the sonographic Murphy sign in suspected acute cholecystitis - PubMed — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6804512/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Hepatobiliary).

explanation: Sustained pain plus inflammation weighs against uncomplicated transient biliary colic.

keyClues.quote: thickened gallbladder wall and surrounding fluid
explanation: Imaging localises the inflammatory process to the gallbladder, supporting cholecystitis.
This makes a common-duct obstructive process less supported. It is not sufficient alone to exclude cholangitis, but the overall localisation favours cholecystitis.

keyConcept.summary: Persistent pain with fever and inflammatory gallbladder changes supports acute cholecystitis.
paragraphs: Cystic-duct obstruction commonly initiates gallbladder distension and inflammation. Common-bile-duct obstruction produces a different pattern and can lead to cholangitis. Use the location of disease rather than treating all gallstone syndromes as equivalent.

commonTraps: Gallstones alone do not prove acute cholecystitis.
recogniseNextTime: The imaging evidence distinguishes inflammation from uncomplicated stone-related colic.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What commonly obstructs the cystic duct in this condition?
followUpQuestions.answer: A gallstone.

questions.stem: A patient recalls the first day of their last normal menstrual period but not the date of conception. Which date conventionally anchors the initial history-based estimate of gestational age?
options: Date of the first antenatal appointment
Last day of the last menstrual period
Date fetal movements were first noticed
First day of the last menstrual period
Date of the first positive pregnancy test
questions.why: Initial menstrual dating conventionally uses the **first day of the last menstrual period**, with ultrasound and clinical context refining dating where appropriate.
distractors: This reflects service attendance rather than pregnancy duration.
Dating convention uses the first day.
This occurs later and varies between pregnancies.
This depends on testing timing and does not define the standard estimate.
lo: Talk to a woman in order to find out their pregnancy story
sources: Pregnancy due date calculator — https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/finding-out/due-date-calculator/

explanation: Gestational age and time since fertilisation are not identical conventions.

keyConcept.summary: Initial menstrual dating conventionally uses the first day of the last menstrual period, with ultrasound and clinical context refining dating where appropriate.
paragraphs: The method assumes a meaningful menstrual history, and irregular cycles can reduce its reliability. A recalled date should not override more appropriate dating assessment. The question concerns the conventional starting point in the history.

commonTraps: Do not equate gestational age exactly with embryo age from fertilisation.
recogniseNextTime: Gestational age and time since fertilisation are not identical conventions.

questions.stem: A university compares five nutritionally adequate lunches using modelled teaching data. Its current lunch contains 8 g saturated fat, 6 g fibre and produces 3.0 kg CO2-equivalent emissions per serving. It wants lower saturated fat, at least as much fibre and lower emissions. Which replacement meets all three aims? Values below are per serving; other nutritional requirements are met.
options: 5 g saturated fat; 4 g fibre; 1.5 kg CO2-equivalent
5 g saturated fat; 8 g fibre; 3.5 kg CO2-equivalent
10 g saturated fat; 8 g fibre; 1.5 kg CO2-equivalent
5 g saturated fat; 8 g fibre; 3.0 kg CO2-equivalent
5 g saturated fat; 8 g fibre; 1.5 kg CO2-equivalent
questions.why: The selected meal reduces saturated fat from 8 to 5 g, maintains or increases fibre from 6 to 8 g and reduces emissions from 3.0 to 1.5 kg CO2-equivalent. It therefore meets every stated criterion in this teaching comparison.
distractors: Saturated fat and emissions fall, but fibre falls below the required 6 g.
The nutrient criteria are met, but emissions rise above the current 3.0 kg per serving.
Fibre and emissions meet the goals, but saturated fat rises from 8 to 10 g.
The nutrient criteria are met, but emissions are unchanged; the aim is a reduction.
lo: Describe the concepts of co-benefits and how promoting a healthy diet can be good for the patient and the planet
sources: BM4 Year 1: Metabolic Disorders (Obesity) - LOs.txt
https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241516648

keyClues.quote: lower saturated fat, at least as much fibre and lower emissions
explanation: Each condition must be satisfied independently. A change that benefits only nutrition or only emissions is insufficient under the stated decision rule.

keyClues.quote: 8 g saturated fat, 6 g fibre and produces 3.0 kg CO2-equivalent
explanation: These are the comparison values: saturated fat must be below 8 g, fibre at least 6 g and emissions below 3.0 kg. Equal emissions do not satisfy a lower-emissions target.

paragraphs: The selected meal reduces saturated fat from 8 to 5 g, maintains or increases fibre from 6 to 8 g and reduces emissions from 3.0 to 1.5 kg CO2-equivalent. It therefore meets every stated criterion in this teaching comparison.

A co-benefit means a change advances more than one goal. These modelled numbers make the comparison answerable; they are not measured estimates for particular foods or proof of long-term health outcomes.

commonTraps: Do not select an option after checking just one favourable number.
recogniseNextTime: Define the baseline, units and decision criteria before ranking interventions.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why can lower emissions alone be insufficient for a sustainable healthy menu?
followUpQuestions.answer: A meal must also meet nutritional and practical requirements; environmental improvement alone does not establish nutritional adequacy.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

editorialRevision.reason: Supply explicit comparative data so only one dietary option meets the health and environmental goals.
editorialRevision.review: AI editorial revision with targeted source checks; not independent clinician sign-off.

questions.assessmentObjective: Use stated nutritional and environmental data to identify a dietary co-benefit while respecting adequacy constraints.

questions.stem: A screening programme lowers the numerical threshold for a positive result. The disease status of the population is unchanged. Which immediate trade-off is generally expected?
options: Higher sensitivity and lower specificity
Unchanged sensitivity and specificity with lower disease prevalence
Higher sensitivity and higher specificity
Lower sensitivity and higher specificity
Lower sensitivity and lower specificity
questions.why: A more permissive threshold captures more true cases but also more false positives: **sensitivity rises while specificity falls**.
distractors: Changing classification does not change the underlying disease prevalence.
A threshold change alone usually trades one against the other.
This would be expected with a stricter positive threshold.
A more permissive threshold does not ordinarily lower sensitivity.
lo: Explain the concepts of sensitivity, specificity and positive and negative predictive values with regard to the accuracy of diagnostic tests
sources: Assessing the Accuracy of Diagnostic Tests - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410404/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Chronic Kidney Injury.

explanation: More people cross the positive boundary: true positives and false positives generally increase.

keyClues.quote: disease status of the population is unchanged
explanation: Changing a test cut-off does not itself change the underlying prevalence of disease.

keyConcept.summary: A more permissive threshold captures more true cases but also more false positives: sensitivity rises while specificity falls.
paragraphs: Consider both missed disease and the consequences of false positives when choosing a threshold. The best balance depends on the condition and downstream testing or treatment, not on maximising one metric alone.

commonTraps: Do not confuse a larger number of positive tests with more disease.
recogniseNextTime: The test classification changes, not the underlying number of diseased people.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which group supplies the denominator for specificity?
followUpQuestions.answer: People without the disease.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: A more permissive threshold captures more true cases but also more false positives: sensitivity rises while specificity falls.

questions.stem: Low-dose aspirin produces a prolonged antiplatelet effect despite a short plasma half-life. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Activation of plasminogen bound to fibrin
Irreversible inhibition of platelet cyclo-oxygenase
Inhibition of vitamin K recycling in the liver
Direct inhibition of circulating thrombin
Reversible blockade of platelet P2Y12 receptors
questions.why: Aspirin **irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase**, reducing thromboxane production for the affected platelet’s remaining life.
distractors: Plasminogen activation promotes fibrin breakdown; it does not explain persistent inhibition of platelet thromboxane synthesis.
Warfarin reduces synthesis of vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors; aspirin acts directly on platelet cyclo-oxygenase.
This is an anticoagulant mechanism, not aspirin’s platelet action.
P2Y12 antagonists inhibit ADP-mediated platelet activation; aspirin instead inhibits thromboxane production.
lo: Outline the mechanism of action of the main drug groups used in acute myocardial infarction, including thrombolytic agents, aspirin, analgesics and oxygen
sources: Salicylic Acid (Aspirin) - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519032/?report=reader
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Ischaemic Heart Disease).

explanation: The biological effect persists in exposed platelets because cyclo-oxygenase has been irreversibly inhibited.
Persistent effect is not explained by prolonged circulating drug levels. Vitamin K antagonism and direct thrombin inhibition are different anticoagulant mechanisms.

keyConcept.summary: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase, reducing thromboxane production for the affected platelet’s remaining life.
paragraphs: Platelets have limited ability to replace the inhibited enzyme. Recovery of function depends substantially on production of new platelets. Distinguish drug half-life from the duration of a biological effect.

commonTraps: A short plasma half-life does not always mean a short pharmacodynamic effect.
recogniseNextTime: The duration reflects persistent target inhibition rather than prolonged drug circulation.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which platelet mediator is reduced?
followUpQuestions.answer: Thromboxane A2.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase, reducing thromboxane production for the affected platelet’s remaining life.

questions.stem: A patient with stable COPD has exertional breathlessness but normal resting oxygenation. Why is long-term oxygen not prescribed solely for breathlessness?
options: Normal resting oxygenation guarantees normal exertional gas exchange
Long-term oxygen reverses fixed airflow obstruction
Its long-term indication depends on documented hypoxaemia and clinical assessment
Breathlessness proves that oxygen delivery is normal
All oxygen treatment must wait for an acute infection
questions.why: Long-term oxygen therapy is assessed using **documented chronic hypoxaemia and relevant clinical criteria**, not the symptom of breathlessness alone.
distractors: Resting results do not guarantee this, but breathlessness alone still does not establish the indication.
It does not reverse the underlying obstructive pathology.
Breathlessness does not establish oxygen status either way.
Oxygen has indications outside infection.
lo: Discuss the indications and effectiveness of long-term oxygen therapy in adults and the implications of this therapy for a patient
sources: NICE NG115: COPD recommendations — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115/chapter/Recommendations
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Failures).

explanation: Breathlessness alone does not establish the chronic resting hypoxaemia used in assessment for long-term oxygen.
Symptoms and oxygenation are related but distinct. Normal resting oxygenation does not guarantee normal exertional gas exchange, nor does breathlessness prove oxygen delivery is normal.

keyConcept.summary: Long-term oxygen therapy is assessed using documented chronic hypoxaemia and relevant clinical criteria, not the symptom of breathlessness alone.
paragraphs: Breathlessness may reflect airflow limitation, deconditioning and other disease. Assess those causes and the person’s needs. Oxygen is a treatment for an identified problem, not a general measure of how severe symptoms feel.

commonTraps: Do not assume more breathlessness always means a lower PaO2.
recogniseNextTime: The symptom and the physiological indication are not interchangeable.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What does long-term oxygen fail to reverse?
followUpQuestions.answer: The underlying fixed airflow obstruction.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Long-term oxygen therapy is assessed using documented chronic hypoxaemia and relevant clinical criteria, not the symptom of breathlessness alone.

questions.stem: A patient with AKI has haematuria. Which urine microscopy finding most strongly supports a glomerular inflammatory source?
options: Fatty casts
Red-cell casts
White-cell casts
Hyaline casts
Muddy brown granular casts
questions.why: **Red-cell casts** form within renal tubules and strongly support bleeding from a glomerular process.
distractors: These suggest heavy proteinuria and a nephrotic pattern.
These support renal inflammation but more often suggest interstitial disease or pyelonephritis.
These can occur in concentrated urine and are not specific for glomerulonephritis.
These favour tubular injury.
lo: Identify the common causes of acute kidney injury, categorising these into pre-renal, renal and post-renal
sources: Urinalysis - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557685/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Acute Kidney Injury.

explanation: The cast type provides localisation beyond a positive dipstick for blood.

keyConcept.summary: Red-cell casts form within renal tubules and strongly support bleeding from a glomerular process.
paragraphs: Casts form in the nephron, unlike free blood from a lower urinary-tract source. No single finding replaces the history and broader assessment, but red-cell casts materially change the differential diagnosis.

commonTraps: Blood on dipstick alone does not localise the source.
recogniseNextTime: The cast type provides localisation beyond a positive dipstick for blood.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which casts are classically associated with acute tubular injury?
followUpQuestions.answer: Muddy brown granular casts.
