questions.stem: Several relatives have early colorectal or endometrial cancer. Tumours show microsatellite instability, and colonoscopy does not reveal hundreds of adenomas. Which inherited pathway defect is most likely?
options: DNA mismatch repair
Type I collagen production
APC-mediated control of beta-catenin
Globin-chain synthesis
CFTR chloride transport
questions.why: The pattern supports **Lynch syndrome**, associated with inherited mismatch-repair dysfunction.
distractors: This causes a connective-tissue disorder, not this tumour signature.
This suggests familial adenomatous polyposis, particularly with a large polyp burden.
This causes haemoglobinopathy rather than the stated cancer predisposition.
This does not explain the cancer pattern or microsatellite instability.
lo: Explain the molecular / genetic basis for an increased risk of cancer in patients with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) and hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC)
sources: Lynch Syndrome - GeneReviews® - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK1211/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Malignancy).

explanation: This familial tumour pattern is characteristic of Lynch syndrome and raises suspicion of inherited mismatch-repair dysfunction.
Failure to repair replication mismatches destabilises repetitive DNA sequences, directly supporting the mismatch-repair pathway.

keyClues.quote: does not reveal hundreds of adenomas
explanation: This weighs against the profuse adenomatous polyposis typical of classical APC-related FAP.

keyConcept.summary: The pattern supports Lynch syndrome, associated with inherited mismatch-repair dysfunction.
paragraphs: The combination of family pattern and tumour testing is informative. Microsatellite instability can also occur in sporadic tumours, so a tumour finding alone does not prove an inherited syndrome.

commonTraps: Do not equate all microsatellite-unstable cancers with germline Lynch syndrome.
recogniseNextTime: Instability at repetitive DNA sequences is a consequence of defective mismatch correction.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which common hereditary syndrome produces hundreds of adenomas?
followUpQuestions.answer: Familial adenomatous polyposis.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The pattern supports Lynch syndrome, associated with inherited mismatch-repair dysfunction.

questions.stem: A test is used in two populations. Sensitivity and specificity are the same, but disease prevalence is higher in population B. Which quantity is generally higher in B?
options: False-positive rate among people without disease
Positive predictive value
Specificity
Positive likelihood ratio
Sensitivity
questions.why: Higher prevalence generally increases **positive predictive value**: a positive result is more likely to represent true disease.
distractors: This is one minus specificity and is therefore unchanged.
The stem explicitly holds specificity constant.
This depends on sensitivity and specificity, which are unchanged.
The stem explicitly holds sensitivity constant.
lo: Explain the concepts of sensitivity, specificity and positive and negative predictive values with regard to the accuracy of diagnostic tests
sources: Diagnostic tests: how to estimate the positive predictive value - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6664615/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Chronic Kidney Injury.

keyClues.quote: Sensitivity and specificity are the same
explanation: These properties are stipulated to remain constant, so neither can be the quantity that rises. The positive likelihood ratio also remains the same.
With more disease in the tested population, a positive result is more likely to be a true positive: positive predictive value rises.

keyConcept.summary: Higher prevalence generally increases positive predictive value: a positive result is more likely to represent true disease.
paragraphs: Predictive values answer the question after a test result is known. Sensitivity and specificity condition on disease status instead. Think about how the pool of true disease changes before applying the test.

commonTraps: Do not confuse the false-positive rate with the proportion of positive tests that are false.
recogniseNextTime: Test operating characteristics are held fixed, isolating the effect of prior disease probability.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What generally happens to negative predictive value as prevalence rises?
followUpQuestions.answer: It falls, with other test characteristics unchanged.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Higher prevalence generally increases positive predictive value: a positive result is more likely to represent true disease.

questions.stem: Digoxin inhibits myocardial Na+/K+ ATPase. Which downstream change contributes to increased contraction strength?
options: Direct inhibition of sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release
Reduced calcium extrusion through the sodium–calcium exchanger
Reduced intracellular sodium concentration
Direct blockade of troponin C calcium binding
Increased calcium extrusion through the sodium–calcium exchanger
questions.why: Increased intracellular sodium reduces the gradient driving calcium extrusion, increasing available intracellular calcium and **contractile force**.
distractors: This would reduce activation of contraction.
Pump inhibition increases, rather than decreases, intracellular sodium.
This would weaken contraction.
This would reduce intracellular calcium available for contraction.
lo: Identify the mode of action and side effects of drugs used to treat heart failure including ACE inhibitors, digoxin, betablockers and diuretics
sources: Digoxin and sodium-dependent inactivation of the sodium-calcium exchanger — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41406234/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

explanation: Trace the sodium gradient before deciding the direction of calcium movement.

keyConcept.summary: Increased intracellular sodium reduces the gradient driving calcium extrusion, increasing available intracellular calcium and contractile force.
paragraphs: Digoxin also increases vagal effects and can slow AV nodal conduction. Its inotropic and conduction effects involve related but distinct mechanisms. The question concerns the pump-mediated inotropic pathway.

commonTraps: Do not describe digoxin as a beta-1 agonist.
recogniseNextTime: Trace the sodium gradient before deciding the direction of calcium movement.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What important conduction effect can it have?
followUpQuestions.answer: Slower AV nodal conduction.

questions.stem: A lung biopsy from a patient with tuberculosis contains epithelioid macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and a central area of caseation. Which inflammatory pattern is present?
options: Acute suppurative inflammation
Fibrinous inflammation
Serous inflammation
Granulomatous inflammation
Eosinophilic inflammation
questions.why: Organised aggregates of activated macrophages with giant cells indicate **granulomatous inflammation**.
distractors: This is dominated by neutrophils and pus formation rather than organised macrophage aggregates.
This describes fibrin-rich exudate rather than the macrophage architecture.
This describes a watery fluid exudate, not an organised granuloma.
This would feature prominent eosinophils rather than the stated structure.
lo: Outline the differences between acute, chronic and granulomatous inflammation in terms of cell constituents, temporal differences and in lung infections including TB
sources: Characteristics of Pulmonary Inflammation in Patients with Different Forms of Active Tuberculosis - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11546853/

explanation: These organised activated macrophage populations are characteristic constituents of granulomas.
Caseating necrosis supports a necrotising granulomatous pattern, compatible with tuberculosis in this context; morphology alone does not identify every possible cause.

keyConcept.summary: Organised aggregates of activated macrophages with giant cells indicate granulomatous inflammation.
paragraphs: Granulomas can occur in infectious and non-infectious disease. Caseation supports tuberculosis in the stated context but is not, by itself, a complete microbiological diagnosis.

recogniseNextTime: The cell types and organisation define the pattern.

Histological grade
Mismatch-repair status
M category
N category

This is a molecular characteristic, not local tumour extent.
This records distant metastases.
This records regional lymph-node involvement.

questions.stem: Over two years, an intervention reduces event risk from 15% to 10%. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one additional event over that period?
questions.why: ARR is 0.15 − 0.10 = 0.05. **NNT = 1/0.05 = 20** over two years.
distractors: This would correspond to an absolute reduction of 1%.
This mistakes the percentage-point reduction for NNT.
This corresponds to an absolute reduction of 10%, not 5%.
This would correspond to an absolute reduction of 2%.

explanation: The absolute risk reduction is 5 percentage points, or 0.05 as a proportion. Five is the reduction in percentage points, not the NNT.
NNT = 1/0.05 = 20 over the stated two-year horizon. It should not be reported as a timeless property of treatment.

Left internal thoracic artery
Right coronary artery
Obtuse marginal artery
First diagonal artery

Lymphatic spread
Perineural extension along a nerve
Haematogenous spread to a distant organ
Direct extension into an adjacent rib

distractors: This concerns spread across a cavity surface, not primarily into a draining node.
This does not best explain a draining lymph node containing tumour.
This describes systemic blood-borne metastasis rather than the regional nodal pattern.
This is local contiguous invasion, not regional nodal involvement.
lo: Explain the different methods by which lung cancer spreads and how this relates to the staging of the disease
sources: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Treatment - NCI — https://www.cancer.gov/types/lung/patient/non-small-cell-lung-treatment-pdq
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Malignancies).

explanation: The named destination is a regional lymph node, supporting drainage through lymphatic channels.
A distant blood-borne deposit is not the spread demonstrated by this case.

keyConcept.summary: Tumour cells can travel through draining lymphatics to regional lymph nodes.
paragraphs: Local invasion, regional nodes and distant metastases describe different aspects of cancer extent. Nodal involvement is important, but does not automatically mean there are distant metastases.

commonTraps: Do not equate any spread with the M category of TNM.
recogniseNextTime: The destination identifies the relevant route of dissemination.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which TNM component records regional nodes?
followUpQuestions.answer: N.

questions.assessmentObjective: Tumour cells can travel through draining lymphatics to regional lymph nodes.

questions.stem: A patient with severe anaemia has normal arterial oxygen saturation but reduced oxygen delivery to tissues. Which quantity is primarily reduced?
options: The arterial CO2 partial pressure
Arterial oxygen content
The affinity of every haemoglobin molecule for oxygen
The inspired oxygen fraction
The percentage saturation of available haemoglobin sites
questions.why: Less haemoglobin means less **oxygen content**, even when the remaining haemoglobin is well saturated.
distractors: This is not the principal explanation for reduced oxygen delivery.
Anaemia does not itself require altered molecular affinity.
No reduction in inspired oxygen is described.
The stem states that saturation is normal.
lo: Explain how the red blood cells are produced, how their turnover is controlled and the physiological consequences of their deficiency or excess
sources: Physiology, Oxygen Transport - PubMed — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30855920/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Anaemia.

explanation: Fewer haemoglobin molecules reduce the amount of oxygen carried per unit blood volume.
The available haemoglobin sites can be normally saturated even when there is too little haemoglobin overall. Saturation and oxygen content are distinct.

keyConcept.summary: Less haemoglobin means less oxygen content, even when the remaining haemoglobin is well saturated.
paragraphs: Oxygen delivery depends on cardiac output and arterial oxygen content. Anaemia can trigger compensatory tachycardia, but that does not immediately replace missing haemoglobin. Distinguish oxygen tension, saturation and content.

commonTraps: Normal pulse oximetry does not exclude inadequate oxygen delivery in anaemia.
recogniseNextTime: Saturation measures occupancy, not the number of haemoglobin binding sites present.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What cardiovascular response can partly compensate?
followUpQuestions.answer: An increase in cardiac output.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Less haemoglobin means less oxygen content, even when the remaining haemoglobin is well saturated.

questions.stem: A patient with breathlessness and ankle oedema has a raised natriuretic peptide. Which investigation most directly assesses ventricular ejection fraction and structural valve disease?
options: Coronary calcium scoring
Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring
Transthoracic echocardiography
Chest radiography
Twelve-lead ECG
questions.why: **Echocardiography** directly evaluates ventricular function and major structural or valve abnormalities.
distractors: This assesses coronary calcification rather than ventricular and valve function.
This characterises blood pressure rather than directly imaging cardiac function.
This may show congestion and heart size but does not directly assess valve function.
This assesses electrical activity and can suggest causes, but does not directly measure ejection fraction.
lo: Identify common tests used to diagnose heart failure, including echocardiography and chest x-ray, relating this to the pathophysiology of the disease
sources: Recommendations | Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management | Guidance | NICE — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng106/chapter/recommendations
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

explanation: This supports further evaluation for heart failure but does not itself define ventricular structure or quantify ejection fraction.

keyClues.quote: ventricular ejection fraction and structural valve disease
explanation: Echocardiography directly evaluates ventricular function and valves. ECG and chest X-ray provide useful supporting information but not these direct structural measurements.

keyConcept.summary: Echocardiography directly evaluates ventricular function and major structural or valve abnormalities.
paragraphs: Natriuretic peptides can support investigation but are affected by multiple clinical factors. Echocardiography helps characterise the underlying cardiac problem rather than replacing clinical assessment with a single biomarker.

commonTraps: A raised peptide level does not identify the specific structural cause.
recogniseNextTime: The desired information is functional and anatomical cardiac imaging.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What does ejection fraction compare?
followUpQuestions.answer: Stroke volume with end-diastolic ventricular volume.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Echocardiography directly evaluates ventricular function and major structural or valve abnormalities.

questions.stem: A smoker says, “I know the risks, but cigarettes help with stress and I am not ready to set a quit date.” What is the most useful next response?
options: Repeat the full list of smoking-related diseases immediately
Choose a quit date for the patient to create commitment
End the discussion until they request medication
Recommend reducing stress first and defer all smoking support
Explore the perceived benefits and concerns, then ask permission to discuss support
questions.why: Explore the person’s **reasons for smoking and ambivalence**, then offer support with permission.
distractors: The patient already acknowledges risk; this may not address the stated barrier.
This bypasses their readiness and participation.
This misses an opportunity to explore motivation and offer support.
Stress can be addressed alongside smoking rather than making it a prerequisite.
lo: Outline the strategies you would adopt to support a patient to quit smoking based on current evidence including evidence based behavioural techniques
sources: Treating tobacco dependence | Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence | Guidance | NICE — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209/chapter/treating-tobacco-dependence
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Malignancies).

explanation: Repeating a disease list does not address the stated barrier or add the missing information in this conversation.
The perceived benefit matters to the patient; exploring it helps identify acceptable alternatives and support.

keyClues.quote: not ready to set a quit date
explanation: Respect readiness while keeping support available. Setting a date for the patient or ending discussion bypasses collaborative exploration.

keyConcept.summary: Explore the person’s reasons for smoking and ambivalence, then offer support with permission.
paragraphs: A discussion can support change without demanding immediate commitment. Understanding the role of smoking makes later planning more realistic. Readiness may change, so an open relationship matters.

commonTraps: Repeating risk information is not always the intervention the patient needs next.
recogniseNextTime: The perceived benefit is a relevant barrier, not a lack of risk information.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What could you ask about smoking and stress?
followUpQuestions.answer: What they find helpful about smoking and what concerns them about continuing.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Explore the person’s reasons for smoking and ambivalence, then offer support with permission.

questions.stem: An infant with severe beta-thalassaemia develops worsening anaemia several months after birth. Which developmental change explains the delayed presentation?
options: Falling gamma-globin production increases dependence on beta globin
Iron absorption begins only after infancy
Erythropoietin production starts only after six months
HbF normally contains two beta chains
Alpha-globin synthesis begins only after birth
questions.why: As **HbF production falls and beta-chain demand rises**, the beta-globin defect becomes more clinically apparent.
distractors: Iron can be absorbed earlier and this is not the globin-switch mechanism.
Erythropoiesis is stimulated before that age.
HbF contains alpha and gamma chains, not beta chains.
Alpha chains are already used in fetal haemoglobin.
lo: Describe the genetic basis of the common haemoglobinopathies, including alpha and beta thalassaemia and sickle cell disease
sources: GeneReviews: Beta-thalassaemia — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1426/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Anaemia.

explanation: The deficit concerns beta-globin production, so symptoms become more marked as adult haemoglobin production depends increasingly on beta chains.
The postnatal decline of gamma-chain-containing HbF exposes the beta-chain deficit. HbF contains gamma, not beta chains; erythropoietin is already produced before this age.

keyConcept.summary: As HbF production falls and beta-chain demand rises, the beta-globin defect becomes more clinically apparent.
paragraphs: HbF contains alpha and gamma chains; the main adult haemoglobin contains alpha and beta chains. A defect can therefore be present from conception yet become prominent only when the affected protein is increasingly required.

commonTraps: Delayed symptoms do not mean the mutation developed after birth.
recogniseNextTime: The timing corresponds to the developmental haemoglobin switch.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What is the usual chain composition of HbF?
followUpQuestions.answer: Two alpha and two gamma chains.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: As HbF production falls and beta-chain demand rises, the beta-globin defect becomes more clinically apparent.

questions.stem: A patient with longstanding hypertension is assessed for target-organ damage. Which result most directly indicates renal involvement rather than a cardiovascular risk factor alone?
options: Increased waist circumference
A family history of hypertension
Raised total cholesterol
Persistently raised urine albumin:creatinine ratio
A high clinic blood-pressure reading
questions.why: Persistent **albuminuria** is evidence of kidney involvement, although its cause requires interpretation.
distractors: This reflects cardiometabolic risk rather than renal damage itself.
This is a risk clue rather than evidence of current organ injury.
This is a cardiovascular risk factor, not direct evidence of renal injury.
This measures pressure but does not by itself prove renal damage.
lo: Carry out a physical examination of a patient with hypertension, including fundoscopy and urine analysis, in order to assess possible end organ damage
sources: Recommendations | Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management | Guidance | NICE — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Hypertension).

explanation: The question separates organ injury from factors that increase the chance of injury.

keyConcept.summary: Persistent albuminuria is evidence of kidney involvement, although its cause requires interpretation.
paragraphs: Hypertension and kidney disease can cause and worsen one another. Confirm an abnormal result appropriately and consider other causes; albuminuria is not uniquely diagnostic of hypertensive nephropathy.

commonTraps: Do not attribute every abnormal renal marker to hypertension without assessment.
recogniseNextTime: The question separates organ injury from factors that increase the chance of injury.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why is persistence relevant?
followUpQuestions.answer: A transient abnormality may have a temporary cause and does not establish chronic damage.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Persistent albuminuria is evidence of kidney involvement, although its cause requires interpretation.

questions.stem: An itchy eczematous rash develops 48 hours after nickel contact. Patch testing reproduces a delayed reaction. Which effector mechanism predominates?
options: IgE-mediated immediate mast-cell degranulation
Antibody-mediated receptor stimulation
Antigen-specific T-cell-mediated inflammation
Circulating immune-complex deposition
Complement deficiency preventing microbial killing
questions.why: Allergic contact dermatitis is a **type IV delayed hypersensitivity** response mediated by T cells.
distractors: This typically develops within minutes rather than the delayed patch-test pattern.
This is a type II functional mechanism rather than delayed contact inflammation.
This is a type III mechanism, not the classic contact response.
This does not explain the reproducible contact reaction.
lo: Explain how a post-streptococcal renal failure relates to the Gel and Coombs classification of hypersensitivity reactions (Types I-IV)
sources: Allergic Contact Dermatitis: Immunopathology and Potential Therapeutic Strategies - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12564274/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Acute Kidney Injury.

explanation: The delayed timing weighs against immediate IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation.

keyClues.quote: Patch testing reproduces a delayed reaction
explanation: Contact hypersensitivity is mediated by antigen-specific T cells rather than a receptor-stimulating antibody or circulating immune-complex mechanism.

keyConcept.summary: Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity response mediated by T cells.
paragraphs: Small chemicals can modify proteins and trigger antigen-specific cellular responses after sensitisation. A positive patch response is assessed on a delayed timescale for this reason.

commonTraps: Not every condition called an allergy is IgE mediated.
recogniseNextTime: The delayed timing is a key distinction from immediate IgE-mediated allergy.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which hypersensitivity type is immediate anaphylaxis?
followUpQuestions.answer: Type I.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity response mediated by T cells.

questions.stem: A patient has resistant hypertension and potassium of 2.8 mmol/L without diuretic use. Testing shows suppressed renin with inappropriately high aldosterone. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Phaeochromocytoma
Secondary hyperaldosteronism from renal artery stenosis
Uncomplicated essential hypertension
Primary adrenal insufficiency
Primary hyperaldosteronism
questions.why: Autonomous aldosterone production causes **sodium retention and potassium loss**, suppressing renin through volume expansion.
distractors: Catecholamine excess does not explain the specific renin–aldosterone pattern.
Renin would usually be increased rather than suppressed.
The hormonal pattern indicates a specific secondary mechanism.
This tends towards low aldosterone, hypotension and hyperkalaemia.
lo: Identify the risk factors predisposing to high blood pressure, including the causes of secondary hypertension
sources: Low-Renin Hypertension - PubMed — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31655771/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Hypertension).

keyClues.quote: potassium of 2.8 mmol/L without diuretic use
explanation: Hypokalaemia without a diuretic raises suspicion of mineralocorticoid excess in a hypertensive patient.
Autonomous aldosterone secretion suppresses renin through sodium retention. Renal artery stenosis usually stimulates renin and secondary aldosterone release.
High aldosterone despite suppressed renin supports primary hyperaldosteronism; primary adrenal insufficiency has the opposite aldosterone direction.

keyConcept.summary: Autonomous aldosterone production causes sodium retention and potassium loss, suppressing renin through volume expansion.
paragraphs: Potassium and medications can affect endocrine testing, so interpretation requires appropriate conditions. The supplied results deliberately establish the physiological pattern rather than relying on hypokalaemia alone.

commonTraps: Not every patient with primary aldosteronism has hypokalaemia.
recogniseNextTime: The paired hormone pattern distinguishes primary from renin-driven secondary aldosteronism.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What happens to distal potassium secretion with aldosterone excess?
followUpQuestions.answer: It increases.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Autonomous aldosterone production causes sodium retention and potassium loss, suppressing renin through volume expansion.

questions.stem: A conventional CD8 T cell recognises a virally infected host cell. Which interaction provides antigen-specific recognition?
options: T-cell receptor binding viral peptide presented by MHC class I
IgE binding an Fc receptor on the infected cell
T-cell receptor binding intact free virus in plasma
Surface immunoglobulin binding peptide on MHC class I
CD8 binding viral peptide presented by MHC class II
questions.why: The TCR recognises **viral peptide–MHC I**, with CD8 acting as a co-receptor.
distractors: This describes a different immune pathway.
Conventional T cells recognise processed peptide–MHC complexes, not free intact antigen in this way.
Surface immunoglobulin is a B-cell receptor, not a T-cell receptor.
Class II is associated with conventional CD4 recognition, and the TCR supplies specificity.
lo: Outline the process of antigen recognition by T-cells
sources: Summary to Chapter 5 - Immunobiology - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK27110/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Malignancies).

explanation: The lymphocyte type determines the usual MHC restriction.

keyConcept.summary: The TCR recognises viral peptide–MHC I, with CD8 acting as a co-receptor.
paragraphs: Intracellular proteins can be processed for presentation on class I molecules. This allows T cells to survey cell contents indirectly. B cells instead can recognise intact antigen through their immunoglobulin receptors.

commonTraps: Do not assign antigen specificity solely to the CD8 molecule.
recogniseNextTime: The lymphocyte type determines the usual MHC restriction.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which MHC class is usually recognised by conventional CD4 T cells?
followUpQuestions.answer: MHC class II.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The TCR recognises viral peptide–MHC I, with CD8 acting as a co-receptor.

questions.stem: Which drug primarily inhibits platelet ADP signalling rather than a coagulation enzyme or clotting-factor synthesis?
options: Warfarin
Dabigatran
Apixaban
Clopidogrel
Unfractionated heparin
questions.why: **Clopidogrel inhibits platelet P2Y12 signalling**, reducing ADP-mediated platelet activation.
distractors: This impairs vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis.
This directly inhibits thrombin.
This directly inhibits factor Xa.
This enhances antithrombin-mediated inhibition of coagulation factors.
questions.module: Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease)
lo: Outline the clotting cascade in order to explain the mechanism of action of anti-coagulant and anti-platelet drugs
sources: P2Y12, a new platelet ADP receptor, target of clopidogrel - PubMed — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15199474/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease).

explanation: Identify the platelet receptor pathway rather than the broader aim of reducing thrombosis.

keyConcept.summary: Clopidogrel inhibits platelet P2Y12 signalling, reducing ADP-mediated platelet activation.
paragraphs: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs act at different parts of haemostasis. Their clinical use depends on the condition and bleeding risk; they are not interchangeable simply because both can reduce thrombotic events.

commonTraps: Do not use “blood thinner” as a substitute for a mechanism.
recogniseNextTime: Identify the platelet receptor pathway rather than the broader aim of reducing thrombosis.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which listed drug directly inhibits factor Xa?
followUpQuestions.answer: Apixaban.

questions.stem: A pathogen consists of nucleic acid within a protein capsid, has no ribosomes and can replicate only using host-cell machinery. Which category best fits?
options: Virus
Mycoplasma
Protozoan
Fungus
Chlamydia
questions.why: The non-cellular structure and lack of ribosomes identify a **virus**, which depends on host machinery for replication.
distractors: These bacteria lack a cell wall but retain ribosomes and cellular machinery.
Protozoa are eukaryotic organisms rather than nucleic-acid capsids.
Fungi are eukaryotic cells with ribosomes and organelles.
These are obligately intracellular bacteria, but have bacterial cellular structures including ribosomes.
lo: Identify the main categories of pathogenic organisms and outline their distinguishing characteristics
sources: Structure and Classification of Viruses - Medical Microbiology - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK8174/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Infections).

keyClues.quote: nucleic acid within a protein capsid
explanation: A capsid containing genetic material is a viral structural organisation, unlike a eukaryotic cell.
Mycoplasma and Chlamydia retain bacterial ribosomes even though their wall or intracellular-growth features differ from other bacteria.
Host dependence supports viral replication, but is insufficient alone to distinguish viruses from all obligately intracellular bacteria.

keyConcept.summary: The non-cellular structure and lack of ribosomes identify a virus, which depends on host machinery for replication.
paragraphs: Classify pathogens by structure as well as growth requirements. Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall but is still a bacterium; Chlamydia is intracellular but is not a virus. These distinctions help explain why antimicrobial targets differ.

commonTraps: Do not classify every obligate intracellular pathogen as a virus.
recogniseNextTime: Obligate intracellular growth alone is insufficient, since some bacteria also require host cells.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why can antibiotics targeting bacterial ribosomes fail against viruses?
followUpQuestions.answer: Viruses lack those bacterial ribosomal targets.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The non-cellular structure and lack of ribosomes identify a virus, which depends on host machinery for replication.

questions.stem: A patient being investigated for possible chronic heart failure has a low natriuretic peptide result. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Heart failure is excluded in every patient
Reduced ejection fraction is confirmed
Heart failure is less likely, but the result must be interpreted in context
The cause of breathlessness is necessarily pulmonary
A valve lesion is identified
questions.why: A low result generally makes heart failure **less likely**, but does not replace contextual interpretation.
distractors: Factors such as obesity and treatment can lower concentrations, so this is too absolute.
A low peptide does not confirm ventricular dysfunction.
Reducing the likelihood of one diagnosis does not establish another.
The biomarker cannot localise a structural valve problem.
lo: Discuss the role of natriuretic peptides in the control of blood volume, and as a diagnostic test
sources: Recommendations | Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management | Guidance | NICE — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng106/chapter/recommendations
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

explanation: This lowers the likelihood of chronic heart failure but does not prove a normal heart or exclude disease in every clinical context.

keyClues.quote: being investigated for possible chronic heart failure
explanation: A biomarker result must be interpreted with the presentation and other findings. It does not independently identify a valve lesion or prove a pulmonary cause.

keyConcept.summary: A low result generally makes heart failure less likely, but does not replace contextual interpretation.
paragraphs: Natriuretic peptides rise with myocardial wall stress but are influenced by clinical circumstances. Consider the whole presentation and the pathway used; a single result should not be turned into a universal exclusion rule.

commonTraps: A test that lowers probability does not prove an alternative diagnosis.
recogniseNextTime: This is a diagnostic-probability question, not an anatomical diagnosis.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which test can assess cardiac structure if concern persists?
followUpQuestions.answer: Echocardiography.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: A low result generally makes heart failure less likely, but does not replace contextual interpretation.

questions.stem: A tumour has an activating mutation in a growth-signalling protein, so the protein signals even without its usual upstream stimulus. Which change best describes this?
options: Proto-oncogene gain of function
A balanced change with no effect on gene activity
Silencing of the growth-signalling pathway
Loss of both copies of a DNA-repair gene
Tumour-suppressor loss of function
questions.why: A **gain-of-function proto-oncogene change** can create an oncogenic growth signal.
distractors: The stem explicitly states increased autonomous activity.
This is opposite to persistent activation.
This impairs repair rather than directly producing the constitutive signal.
This removes a brake rather than activating the growth-promoting signal described.
lo: Explain how gene mutations in oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes may lead to the development of malignancy
sources: What Is Cancer? - NCI — https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/understanding/what-is-cancer
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Malignancies (Breast Cancer).

explanation: Increased activity in a growth-promoting pathway describes gain of function, not loss of a tumour suppressor or DNA-repair function.

keyClues.quote: signals even without its usual upstream stimulus
explanation: The mutation bypasses the normal requirement for a growth signal; this is neither a neutral change nor pathway silencing.

keyConcept.summary: A gain-of-function proto-oncogene change can create an oncogenic growth signal.
paragraphs: One activating allele may be sufficient at the cellular level, although tumour formation usually requires additional changes. This differs from the common two-hit model used to explain many tumour suppressors.

commonTraps: Do not apply the two-hit rule identically to every cancer gene.
recogniseNextTime: Constitutive signalling identifies inappropriate activation rather than loss of a suppressive function.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What is an oncogene?
followUpQuestions.answer: A gene whose altered activity promotes tumour development.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: A gain-of-function proto-oncogene change can create an oncogenic growth signal.

questions.stem: A patient has a documented DNACPR recommendation and now develops a treatable chest infection without cardiac arrest. What is the correct interpretation of the recommendation?
options: It removes the need to discuss the current illness with the patient
It excludes antibiotics for any future infection
It concerns CPR; other treatment should follow the separate clinical and agreed care plan
It requires all care to be symptom-only
It means the patient has refused every emergency intervention
questions.why: **DNACPR concerns cardiopulmonary resuscitation**, not automatic withdrawal of other appropriate care.
distractors: The patient should remain involved according to their abilities and wishes.
DNACPR does not itself prohibit antibiotics.
Other treatment limits must be considered and documented separately.
A CPR recommendation is not a blanket refusal of care.
lo: Discuss the concept of treatment escalation and advanced planning including the decision not to resuscitate
sources: Resuscitation Council UK: CPR recommendations, DNACPR and ReSPECT — https://www.resus.org.uk/public-resource/cpr-decisions-and-dnacpr
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — End of Life.

explanation: The recommendation concerns cardiopulmonary resuscitation specifically; it is not a blanket refusal of treatment.

keyClues.quote: treatable chest infection without cardiac arrest
explanation: The current problem should be assessed and treated according to the patient’s wishes and wider care plan. CPR is not the intervention under consideration.

keyConcept.summary: DNACPR concerns cardiopulmonary resuscitation, not automatic withdrawal of other appropriate care.
paragraphs: Emergency care planning can record broader priorities and treatment limits. Read the whole plan and reassess the current problem rather than expanding one recommendation beyond its scope.

commonTraps: Do not treat DNACPR as a synonym for “do not treat”.
recogniseNextTime: The current decision concerns infection treatment, not whether to attempt CPR.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Where should broader treatment limits be recorded?
followUpQuestions.answer: In an appropriate emergency or treatment-escalation plan, with relevant discussions documented.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: DNACPR concerns cardiopulmonary resuscitation, not automatic withdrawal of other appropriate care.

questions.stem: An adult with capacity asks that their diagnosis not be shared with family. There is no legal requirement or overriding public-interest reason to disclose. A relative phones for details. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Disclose because the caller is the closest relative
Maintain confidentiality while offering to listen to the relative’s concerns
Confirm the diagnosis but withhold treatment details
Refuse to listen to any information from the relative
Ask the relative to promise not to tell anyone before disclosing
questions.why: Respect the patient’s **confidentiality**. Receiving concerns is different from revealing clinical information.
distractors: Being a relative does not automatically confer access.
Even confirming the diagnosis would disclose confidential information.
Listening need not involve disclosing patient information.
A promise does not replace the patient’s consent or another lawful basis.
lo: Be familiar with the principles of good medical practice and the reasoning behind them as defined by the GMC
sources: GMC: Disclosing personal information framework — https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/the-professional-standards/confidentiality/disclosing-patients-personal-information-a-framework
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

keyClues.quote: asks that their diagnosis not be shared with family
explanation: The patient has explicitly withheld permission; being the closest relative does not override that choice.

keyClues.quote: no legal requirement or overriding public-interest reason
explanation: The stem excludes a justification for disclosure without consent.
You can receive concerns without disclosing confidential facts in return. Maintaining confidentiality does not require refusing to listen.

paragraphs: You can explain confidentiality in general terms and seek the patient’s permission for future involvement. A relative’s concern may be valuable without making them entitled to a diagnostic update.

commonTraps: Do not confuse listening with disclosure.
recogniseNextTime: The stem removes the main alternative bases that could justify disclosure without consent.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Can the patient authorise limited information sharing?

questions.stem: Several weeks after a bereavement, a person has waves of sadness and poor sleep but still experiences some enjoyment and maintains basic functioning. They deny suicidal thoughts. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
options: Diagnose major depression from the presence of sadness alone
Prescribe an antidepressant solely because sleep is disturbed
Reassure them that no future assessment will be needed
Set a fixed deadline by which grief should end
Explore their experience, support and functioning, and offer follow-up without assuming a disorder
questions.why: The pattern can occur in **grief**, but assessment should explore distress, support, functioning and changing risk.
distractors: Sadness after loss does not by itself establish major depression.
Sleep disturbance alone does not establish the indication.
Symptoms and risks can change, so access to follow-up matters.
Grief varies and is not governed by a universal short timetable.
lo: Discuss the physical and psychological effects of loss and grief on the patient, carer, and healthcare professional across different cultures.
sources: Get help with grief after bereavement or loss — https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/grief-bereavement-loss/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — End of Life.

explanation: Grief often fluctuates; sadness alone is insufficient to diagnose major depression.

keyClues.quote: some enjoyment and maintains basic functioning
explanation: Preserved enjoyment and functioning support an initial exploratory and supportive response rather than diagnosing from one symptom.
This contributes to risk assessment but does not remove the need for follow-up or establish a fixed timetable for recovery.

keyConcept.summary: The pattern can occur in grief, but assessment should explore distress, support, functioning and changing risk.
paragraphs: Normal grief can be painful and still merit support. Avoid both immediate medicalisation and dismissal. Review is appropriate if symptoms persist, worsen or substantially impair functioning, or if safety concerns arise.

commonTraps: “Not automatically a disorder” does not mean “no help needed”.
recogniseNextTime: The overall pattern matters more than a single symptom such as sadness.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What should prompt earlier reassessment?
followUpQuestions.answer: Worsening function, escalating distress or suicidal thoughts.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The pattern can occur in grief, but assessment should explore distress, support, functioning and changing risk.

questions.stem: A patient with a learning disability presents with new weight loss and abdominal pain. The clinician attributes both to their disability without taking a history or examining them. Which error is illustrated?
options: Regression to the mean
Confounding by indication
Lead-time bias
Diagnostic overshadowing
Recall bias
questions.why: **Diagnostic overshadowing** occurs when new symptoms are attributed to an existing disability or diagnosis without adequate assessment.
distractors: This describes statistical movement of extreme measurements, not the clinical attribution error.
This concerns treatment choices associated with prognosis in observational research.
This concerns earlier diagnosis changing measured survival.

questions.stem: Two siblings ask about rheumatoid arthritis risk because their mother is affected. One smokes and the other does not. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Inherited susceptibility and smoking can both contribute to RA risk
Smoking causes OA but has no association with RA
RA follows a fully penetrant single-gene dominant inheritance pattern
Only repetitive manual work determines whether RA develops
A normal rheumatoid factor result eliminates future RA risk
questions.why: RA is multifactorial. Family history and HLA-related susceptibility contribute, and smoking is an established environmental risk factor; neither exposure makes disease inevitable.
distractors: Smoking is also relevant to RA susceptibility.
RA is polygenic and does not show fully penetrant Mendelian inheritance.
Occupational loading is relevant to some OA, but does not explain autoimmune RA risk alone.
Autoantibody status cannot guarantee that RA will never develop.

Prolonged standing at a counter with the knees extended
Repeated kneeling and squatting while laying flooring
Frequent seated work with the knees held at a right angle
Repeated short walks between workstations on level ground

questions.stem: A hairdresser with RA has morning hand stiffness and fatigue. Disease treatment is being adjusted. She wants to keep working, but repeated gripping early in the day is difficult. What is the most appropriate occupational approach?
options: Recommend complete absence from work until morning stiffness resolves
Keep all duties unchanged while waiting to judge the DMARD adjustment
Agree task and schedule adjustments with occupational support, guided by her goals
Recommend a permanent move to lighter work before assessing task adaptations
Use grip strength alone to determine fitness for all hairdressing duties

distractors: A symptom-free state is not always required for safe work; first assess feasible adaptations and the patient’s goals.

One strength measure cannot capture fatigue, timing, task demands and practical adaptations.

Acute gout affecting a single joint

A routine symmetrical RA flare

Septic arthritis

questions.stem: A 52-year-old develops severe redness and pain at the first MTP joint overnight. He has had two similar self-limiting attacks. Serum urate measured during the attack is 320 micromol/L. What is the best interpretation?

The result establishes osteoarthritis

This result proves septic arthritis
The result does not exclude gout; urate can be lower during a flare

questions.stem: A patient with longstanding seropositive RA develops progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. Examination reveals fine bibasal inspiratory crackles; CT demonstrates a fibrotic interstitial pattern. Which manifestation can account for these findings?

Bronchiectasis
Pulmonary embolism
Rheumatoid pleuritis without parenchymal involvement

questions.stem: A patient with active RA has haemoglobin 103 g/L, MCV 88 fL, low serum iron, low transferrin and raised ferritin. Kidney function is normal and there is no evidence of bleeding. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?

An inherited inability to produce haemoglobin A from birth
Autoimmune destruction of platelets
Absent intrinsic factor prevents vitamin B12 absorption
Loss of erythrocytes from an acute large haemorrhage

distractors: A new inflammatory pattern in active RA is not evidence of a congenital haemoglobin disorder.
Platelet destruction does not explain low haemoglobin with iron restriction.
B12 deficiency more often causes macrocytosis and does not explain this iron pattern.
The stated history and iron indices favour inflammation rather than acute haemorrhage.

questions.stem: In a patient with established RA, a finger is flexed at the PIP joint and hyperextended at the DIP joint. Which deformity is described?

questions.stem: After a long period of limb immobilisation, bone mass in that limb decreases. Which bone-cell function most directly links reduced mechanical loading to altered remodelling?

questions.stem: The graph is a schematic neuronal action potential. During the shaded interval X, which channel change is most responsible for preventing an immediate second action potential of normal amplitude?

Increased voltage-gated potassium conductance alone
Closure of sodium channels into a resting, immediately available state
Opening of postsynaptic GABA-A chloride channels
An accelerated sodium–potassium pump current
questions.why: X falls during early repolarisation, when many voltage-gated sodium channels remain inactivated. They must recover from inactivation as the membrane repolarises before they can support another normal regenerative upstroke.
distractors: Persisting potassium conductance contributes to reduced excitability, particularly later in the relative refractory period. Sodium-channel inactivation is the main reason another normal upstroke cannot immediately occur in the early interval shown.
A resting closed sodium channel can reopen with sufficient depolarisation. An inactivated channel must first recover before it can participate in another upstroke.
Inhibitory synaptic input can reduce excitability, but it is not an intrinsic channel-state change produced by the preceding axonal action potential.
The pump maintains ion gradients over time. Recovery of voltage-gated sodium channels, rather than pump speed, principally determines this immediate refractory interval.

questions.stem: Two illustrative cerebral pressure–flow responses are shown. Over the plotted pressure range, which statement best explains trace A?
options: Arterioles progressively dilate as perfusion pressure rises
Arteriolar resistance changes to keep flow approximately constant
The trace proves that flow–metabolism coupling is absent
Vascular resistance stays fixed as perfusion pressure rises
Flow is determined by arterial carbon dioxide alone
questions.why: Trace A is a plateau: flow remains approximately constant as perfusion pressure changes. With autoregulation intact, arterioles adjust resistance. Trace B illustrates a more pressure-passive response. The plotted range is illustrative and does not define universal clinical limits.
distractors: Progressive dilatation as pressure rises would amplify rather than buffer the increase in flow.
Pressure autoregulation and flow–metabolism coupling are distinct; this graph does not test whether metabolic coupling is present.
With fixed resistance, flow would generally rise as perfusion pressure rises, resembling B.
Carbon dioxide affects flow, but the pressure–flow plateau demonstrates a response to changing perfusion pressure and does not show exclusive carbon-dioxide control.

questions.stem: A commissioning group compares two MS services over the same time horizon. Service B costs £12,000 more per patient and provides an additional 0.4 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs). What is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of B compared with A?
options: £48,000 per QALY
£12,000 per QALY
£30,000 per QALY
£3,000 per QALY
£4,800 per QALY
questions.why: The ICER is the difference in costs divided by the difference in QALYs: £12,000 / 0.4 = £30,000 per QALY. It describes the extra cost of one additional QALY; affordability, uncertainty and distributive concerns also inform allocation.
distractors: This does not follow from the stated incremental costs and benefits.
£12,000 is the incremental cost, without adjustment for the 0.4-QALY gain.
The calculation is 12,000 / 0.4, not 12,000 / 4.
Multiplying cost by QALYs gives £4,800 but the incremental ratio divides additional cost by additional health gain.

questions.stem: An NHS panel has enough funding for only one of two effective neurological services. It considers total health gain, severity of need, equal access and the care displaced by each choice. Which ethical principle most directly concerns the fair distribution of these limited resources?
options: Distributive justice
Veracity
Fidelity
Respect for autonomy
Confidentiality
questions.why: Distributive justice asks how benefits and burdens should be shared fairly. Cost-effectiveness contributes evidence about health gain and opportunity cost, while explicit ethical reasoning addresses competing claims such as need and equitable access.
distractors: Veracity concerns truthfulness; transparent allocation uses it but the fairness question is justice.
Fidelity concerns keeping commitments and maintaining trust, rather than the distribution rule itself.
Autonomy concerns individuals making informed choices; it does not itself determine a fair distribution across a population.
Confidentiality governs information handling rather than allocation between patient groups.

questions.stem: A student compares population patterns of multiple sclerosis. Which pattern is most consistent with its established epidemiology?
options: Onset mainly after 85, with equal numbers of men and women
Onset mainly in childhood, with no geographical variation
Onset commonly in young adulthood, with women affected more often than men
Onset commonly in young adulthood, with men affected more often than women

Both the usual age pattern and absence of geographical variation are incorrect.
The age range fits, but women are affected more often.

questions.stem: A woman with MS asks whether her identical twin will inevitably develop the same condition. Which explanation best reflects MS aetiology?
options: MS follows a fully penetrant autosomal dominant pattern
Genetic susceptibility interacts with environmental exposures; an identical twin is at increased risk but disease is not inevitable
MS is directly contagious between household members
MS is caused by a vitamin deficiency in every patient
MS occurs only after occupational exposure to a specific solvent
questions.why: Family and twin observations support inherited susceptibility, but incomplete concordance shows that genes alone are insufficient. EBV infection has a strong association with MS risk; smoking, vitamin D-related factors and other exposures also contribute to a multifactorial model.

Association with infections such as EBV does not mean MS itself is transmitted between people.
Vitamin D status is an associated risk factor, not a universal sufficient cause.
No single occupational exposure is necessary and sufficient for MS.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old teacher with MS has mild leg weakness but severe fatigue. She worries about keeping her job, taking a mortgage and starting a family. Which approach best assesses the illness across her life course?
options: Base planning solely on the number of MRI lesions
Assume family planning is irrelevant until physical disability is severe
Estimate future disability from her current walking distance alone
Discuss employment only once she can no longer work
Explore her current roles and future goals, and review how symptoms and support affect each over time

Walking captures only part of neurological impact and cannot establish her future trajectory.

Confirm that severe disability within a few years is inevitable
Explain the variability of MS, explore the plans that matter to her, and arrange ongoing personalised advice
Recommend that her partner make all future decisions

questions.stem: During a review, a patient with a chronic neurological disorder attends with her husband, who answers every question. She has capacity and communicates slowly. What is the best first step to understand her own experience?
options: Restrict questions to symptoms that can be objectively measured
Exclude the husband permanently without asking her preference
Address her directly, allow time to answer, and ask how she would like her husband involved
Assume slow speech means she cannot provide a useful account
Use the husband as the sole historian to save time

distractors: Personal impact includes experiences and priorities not captured by examination.
She may value his involvement; establish her wishes rather than impose a blanket rule.
Communication speed does not establish cognitive inability or lack of capacity.
A relative’s account can add information but should not replace the patient’s voice when she can participate.

Loss of colour perception in both eyes
An isolated refractive abnormality in one eye
A fixed defect in the left visual field
A cataract producing monocular ghosting

questions.stem: Light in the right eye produces brisk constriction of both pupils. When the light is swung to the left eye, both pupils become relatively larger. Eye movements are normal. Where is the most likely deficit?

Left oculomotor parasympathetic fibres
Right optic nerve
Both abducens nerves
Left afferent visual pathway, usually the optic nerve

questions.stem: In England and Wales, a woman with mild dementia can understand, retain and weigh information and communicate decisions about a blood test and sharing its results. She agrees to the test but declines disclosure to her daughter. No legal duty or serious-harm justification for disclosure is identified. The daughter asks to consent and receive the results as next of kin. What is the best response?
options: Obtain the daughter’s consent and disclose because she is listed as next of kin
Obtain the woman’s consent but disclose routinely to the daughter because she provides daily care

Delay the blood test until the woman and daughter agree on disclosure

distractors: Next-of-kin status does not confer authority to consent for a capacitous adult or an automatic right to confidential results.

The woman has consented to the test; disagreement about family disclosure does not by itself invalidate that consent.

Extinction of a previously conditioned response

questions.stem: A patient had fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations and parkinsonism. The cortical section shows rounded brown intraneuronal inclusions on immunostaining. Which protein most likely forms these inclusions?

Amyloid-beta
Tau
TDP-43
Alpha-synuclein
questions.why: The clinical syndrome and rounded neuronal inclusions support dementia with Lewy bodies. Lewy bodies contain aggregated alpha-synuclein. The diagnosis rests on the clinical and pathological context, not on brown staining alone, because the stain colour is not protein-specific without knowing the antibody.
distractors: Prion disease usually causes a rapidly progressive syndrome with spongiform pathology; these inclusions and the clinical pattern point to Lewy body disease.
Amyloid-beta is primarily found in extracellular plaques rather than these characteristic neuronal inclusions.
Tau is the main component of neurofibrillary tangles; rounded Lewy inclusions and this syndrome point to alpha-synuclein.
TDP-43 inclusions occur in several disorders, especially some frontotemporal degenerations and motor neuron disease; the clinical and pathological context here favours Lewy pathology.
